articles.title: Fixated on AI, the world has forgotten what is staring it in the face: nuclear annihilation | Simon Tisdall
articles.body:
Humankind has fearfully and sometimes joyfully anticipated the end of the world ever since it began. The Bible’s Book of Revelation speaks of “end times”, a period of tribulation, war, famine, plague, floods and environmental catastrophe that may seem a less absurd prospect today than perhaps it once did. Islam, too, posits a fateful day of judgment or day of reckoning. Christian evangelicals believe that, in the final rapture, a chosen few – the righteous or the “elect” – will be saved while sinners burn. It’s a minority view. Matthew’s gospel predicts most people will defy, ignore or ridicule warnings of imminent Armageddon. Peter, another of Jesus’s disciples, agreed: “In the last days, scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires.” Yet such worldly scepticism does not mean a universal cataclysm is less likely. It may make it more probable.
Donald Trump’s blanket denials of the dangers ostensibly posed by artificial intelligence, whose uncontrolled development is seen by some as the latest harbinger of apocalypse, could be interpreted as fulfilling Peter’s prophecy. This US president, the nearest thing the world has to a one-man doomsday machine, is a great one for scoffing and evil desires. In Robert Harris’s 2019 novel, The Second Sleep, a worried scientist lists half a dozen ways the world might end. They include devastating climate change, pandemic disease, a giant asteroid collision with Earth, or some other overwhelming calamity. Few heed the fictional scientist’s fears. In the event, what destroys him and almost everybody else is a disturbingly plausible cyber crash – a global digital and internet meltdown.
While arguments rage over whether large language models will acquire consciousness and moral agency – and the power to delete humanity – existential AI threats remain, as of now, open to mitigation. In sharp contrast, extraordinary complacency surrounds the most pressing, avoidable and proven human-made threat to life on Earth. It is as if the world has been seized by collective deafness and by a blind refusal to see what’s staring it in the face. This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating, global proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing real-time “end times” closer to home by the day. The question increasingly is not “if” but “when” limited or full-scale nuclear warfare will erupt. Eighty-one years after Hiroshima, how much longer can our luck hold?
Alarm bells are ringing, if only people would listen. Desperate Vladimir Putin recently threatened to deploy Russia’s entire nuclear arsenal, comprising about 4,400 warheads, against Nato countries if they activated a supposed plan to invade the Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad. He offered no evidence for his claim, and it’s true that the frequent Kremlin nuclear sabre-rattling since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine went pear-shaped has diminished Moscow’s credibility. Yet that in itself is destabilising. To work, nuclear deterrence relies on an adversary believing the threat is real. Disbelief invites miscalculation. At the same time, Putin’s inability to halt Ukraine’s conventional drone and missile attacks deep inside Russia may be edging him closer to pressing the nuclear button, possibly in the form of low-yield tactical or “battlefield” nukes.
Trump’s bottom-line justification for the illegal US-Israel war on Iran is his wilfully mendacious claim that Tehran was weeks away from obtaining the bomb. He claims to be protecting the world from nuclear war. Yet his reckless threat, issued at the UN, to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” implies a possible US nuclear attack. Trump’s hypocrisy is stunning. The US is upgrading its nuclear arsenal of 3,700 warheads and may resume nuclear tests. It unreservedly supports Israel’s hidden nuclear weapons programme. And Trump is pursuing a lucrative deal with Saudi Arabia, another bitter foe of Iran, to provide civilian nuclear technology that he knows could be repurposed to make weapons. That has prompted regional countries such as Turkey and Egypt to consider going nuclear.
Similarly perilous trends are evident across Asia. North Korea’s great panjandrum, Kim Jong-un, has succeeded in gaining de facto international acceptance of his country’s status as a nuclear weapons state. South Korea said in August that Pyongyang now possesses up to 120 warheads – which Kim brandishes to intimidate neighbours. All but discarded are the twin principles that underpinned the west’s postwar Korea policy: reunification and denuclearisation. Heedless of first-term humiliations, Trump is again seeking a summit with Kim, whom he bizarrely terms a friend. “As long as I’m around, he [Kim] is going to be fine,” he boasted. Japan and South Korea don’t share his confidence. Both debate acquiring nuclear weapons in self-defence. Meanwhile, China’s president, Xi Jinping, having again bamboozled a fawning Trump at their Washington summit, is reportedly building nukes like there’s no tomorrow – which, at this rate, there may not be.
Addressing the UN general assembly, secretary-general António Guterres warned the world has reached “the most dangerous nuclear moment” since 1989. Global military spending reached nearly $3tn last year, while AI is increasing uncertainty over nuclear command-and-control, the UN was told. Annual spending on nukes is up by 20%. In a new paper published by the non-partisan Arms Control Association (ACA), Daryl Kimball, the head of the ACA in Washington, bemoaned the absence of high-level disarmament talks between the main nuclear powers and the lapsing of strategic arms limitation treaties. “The nuclear sword of Damocles still hangs over all of us. The threat has become more complex, and in the absence of new arms-control breakthroughs, we are headed for an unprecedented three-way buildup of Chinese, Russian, and US nuclear forces,” Kimball warned.
The fragmentation of the rules-based international order provides aggravating context. Trump-era blasphemies – that might makes right, that international law and the non-proliferation treaty’s binding obligation to disarm can be ignored, and that the UN charter and human rights norms don’t apply to authoritarian “strongman” leaders – all grease the slide into nuclear anarchy. Unresolved forever wars in Palestine, Iran, Ukraine, Myanmar, Yemen and Sudan are base components of a third world war. Potentially earth-shattering, too, is the fast-developing contest for control of space, notably the race to build nuclear-powered lunar bases. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, under which more than 130 countries agreed the moon is no one’s property, is now routinely flouted by both governments and billionaires such as Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos. The weaponising of space by the US and others advances rapidly. Russia, for example, is reportedly developing an orbiting nuclear-armed anti-satellite weapon.
If the human race really is determined to bring the heavens crashing down in a mad dash for eschatological self-destruction, this is the surest, quickest way to go about it. More surprising than the irresponsible behaviour of politicians is the deafening public silence, the absence of large-scale protest in much of the world, the complacency, bordering on indifference, that accompanies this global march to oblivion. If and when a final reckoning comes, individuals who stayed silent will be complicit in their own undoing. Hiroshima is not a shrine. It’s the future.
- Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

articles.title: European Leaders Back Zelenskyy After Trump's Diesel Deal; Russia, Ukraine Continue To Trade Strikes
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump announced an energy cease-fire between Russia and Ukraine, following his earlier decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports and his subsequent call for a change in leadership in Kyiv.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," he wrote on October 11 on Truth Social. "Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
Shortly after, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv supported the initiative and was waiting for details from Washington. He had earlier signaled a willingness to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, provided Moscow stopped attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
"It is important that Russia support it as well," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "Ukraine always FULLY supports steps toward de-escalation, the protection of lives, and the decisions needed to end the war and guarantee lasting peace."
There was no immediate confirmation from Moscow of Trump's announcement, which came amid continued Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities and Ukrainian drone attacks on technology facilities inside Russia.
Previously, the Kremlin has been rejecting calls for any cease-fire agreements, seeking to pressure Kyiv into unfavorable deal by heavily targeting energy sites in Ukraine and leaving thousands without heat or electricity amid freezing temperatures in winter.
Trump's latest statement came two days after Russian President Vladimir Putin and Trump announced a deal to temporarily loosen curbs on Russian diesel exports, a decision Zelenskyy characterized as a sign of US "weakness" and a "gift" to Putin.
The Ukrainian president argued that renewed Russian energy revenues would encourage Moscow to prolong its long-running invasion, now in its 56th month.
Trump later said that Ukraine should "get a new leader," blaming Zelenskyy for the lack of a deal to end Russia's war against his country and demanding Kyiv "damn well stop" hitting Russian oil refineries amid a global energy shortage largely caused by the US war with Iran.
The US president made ending Russia's war on Ukraine war a priority when he began his current term in January 2025, but Kyiv and Moscow remain far apart in their negotiating positions.
The Kremlin has been offering no concessions and has been sticking to hard-line demands including Russian control over the portion of the Donbas it has been unable to seize in battle.
In addition, Russia has continued its relentless bombardment of Ukrainian regions. Since the beginning of this year, however, Kyiv has increasingly responded with a campaign of its own.
Ukrainian long-range strikes have been targeting Russian military and oil-refinery facilities in an effort to curb revenues for the invasion.
"Ukraine will be ready to stop attacks on Russian refineries if Russia stops attacking our energy infrastructure. Any de-escalation steps must be mutual and with real guarantees," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram on October 11.
Moscow Continues Daily Strikes, Kyiv Targets Yandex
Hours after Trump's announcement of the energy cease-fire, Ukrainian officials reported fresh Russian strikes on the country's civilian and energy infrastructure.
In the country's second-largest city of Kharkiv, at least three people were killed and nine others injured when Russian forces struck near a local grocery store, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
Zelenskyy said Russia had also targeted energy infrastructure in the region. "Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian Shahed drones all day today," he added in his daily video address.
Three more people were killed in a jet-powered drone strike in Ukraine's western region of Ivano-Frankivsk. The attack damaged a local hotel and left three other people injured, according to the city authorities.
Earlier in the day, in Slovyansk, in the eastern Donetsk region, a Russian air strike damaged two apartment buildings, destroying an entire entrance section of a five-story block. At least four people were reported injured, while rescuers worked to free residents trapped in apartments, according to RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service.
"I can't breathe," local resident Svitlana told RFE/RL at the site of the aftermath with her hands shaking. She was walking on crutches, she said, adding that rescuers have carried her down from her ruined apartment on the fourth floor.
"I feel bad," Svitlana said. "We were sleeping... Now nothing in the apartment is left intact."
Elsewhere, in the southeastern city of Dnipro, Russian drones damaged an apartment building and set fire to warehouses and vehicles, injuring four people, including two eight-year-old girls, according to regional authorities.
In the southern port city of Odesa, an attack late on October 10 damaged a two-story residential building, destroying three apartments and setting the roof ablaze.
Ukraine has meanwhile continued its retaliatory strikes on Russian technology infrastructure, targeting facilities operated by Yandex, the country's leading Internet search and technology company.
A drone strike on October 11 forced the complete shutdown of a Yandex data center in Russia's Vladimir region.
Yandex said the facility had ceased operations and that some of its services were unavailable as a result. It reported no casualties. According to Russian reports, Yandex's taxi and food delivery services were disrupted in Moscow following the drone attacks.
Often described as the Russian Google, Yandex operates widely used search, mapping, and other digital services, and is a major developer of artificial intelligence. Its data centers support both consumer services and computing infrastructure used to develop AI models, making their disruption potentially significant for Russia's technology sector.
The latest attack followed a strike on Yandex's Sasovo facility in the Ryazan region overnight on October 7-8, which reportedly disabled two of the company's three main AI-development supercomputers, and another on October 9 that knocked out part of its data center in Kaluga.
European Leaders Back Ukraine
Amid Trump's harshest criticism of Zelenskyy since the two had improved ties following a highly contentious meeting at the White House in February 2025, European leaders have reaffirmed their support for the Ukrainian president and country's defensive efforts.
"This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas wrote on X on October 10, condemning the diesel agreement and warning it would increase Moscow's war revenues.
She added that EU foreign ministers planned to approve new sanctions listings on October 12. Meanwhile, some of the bloc's biggest member states, including Germany, confirmed they would maintain their strict sanctions regime despite Washington's shift.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo described Trump's agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin as a "terrible disappointment," while Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson noted that the upcoming EU package would target 1,600 entities within Russia's military-industrial complex.
Over the past day, Zelenskyy had a series of phone with French President Emmanuel Macron, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, discussing air defense and continued pressure on Moscow.
“The Russians must feel that they will have no capacity left to prolong the war,” Zelenskyy said after speaking with Macron.
He also confirmed that Finland would deliver specialized ammunition for Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets in the coming days to assist in intercepting Russian Shahed drones.
Separately, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on October 10 that “the past 24 hours had been difficult for Ukraine,” according to Downing Street, adding that the UK would continue strengthening sanctions on Russia independently.
Meanwhile, the US-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) warned in an assessment on October 9 that the unilateral easing of restrictions would benefit Russia's war effort without securing a comparable concession from Moscow.
In a follow-up assessment on October 10, the think tank noted that Putin utilized the call to blame Ukraine for stalled peace talks, citing alleged Ukrainian strikes on Russian election infrastructure during September's State Duma elections.
ISW said that this allegation was unsupported by evidence and that Putin's "unchanged war aims demonstrates the Kremlin’s continued unwillingness to accept any compromised peace proposals on any terms that fall short of fulfilling Russia’s maximalist demands of Ukraine’s complete capitulation."

articles.title: Middle East crisis live: Houthis warn passengers against using Saudi airport after deadly attack on Riyadh
articles.body:
Following yesterday’s attack on Riyadh international airport that killed 12 people and injured hundreds, the site was hit again on Sunday. Authorities said an “unidentified projectile” struck Terminal 4 at King Khalid International Airport. Air defenses also “intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile” in the vicinity of the airport.
An Egyptian flight attendant, a Syrian woman, and an Indian national were among the 12 killed in yesterday’s Saudi airport attack. The Egyptian woman killed was identified as Azza Ramzy, 28. The Syrian woman was identified as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.
The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement that today’s attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh “resulted in injuries” but did not specify how many.
Yemen’s Houthis have claimed responsibility for both Saturday and Sunday’s attacks on Riyadh Airport. The group said on Sunday they had targeted Riyadh’s airport several times as well as Saudi energy facilities, a day after Saturday’s deadly attack.
The United Arab Emirates issued a statement in solidarity with Saudi Arabia, expressing support for “all measures aimed at safeguarding the kingdom’s security and stability”. The UAE message is significant given the major rupture in relations this year.
The Houthis this morning issued a warning to travelers and airlines to stay away from Saudi airports following yesterday’s attack. A Houthi military spokesman warned the public to “take our warning seriously” and also claimed that “Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions”.
The attacks on Riyadh airport came just before a major oil summit, the World Petroleum Congress, scheduled for this week. The repeated attacks have temporarily halted oil flows and driven up global oil prices. The CEOs of major companies Shell, ExxonMobil, BP, TotalEnergies had been due to attend the summit but given the attacks, it’s unclear if executives will take the risk.
Indian national dies from injuries following Riyadh airport attack
An Indian national wounded in yesterday’s Houthi airport attack in Riyadh has died from his injuries, the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said in a statement.
“It is learnt that one Indian national injured in the Riyadh attack has unfortunately lost his life today,” the embassy said. “We convey our heartfelt condolences to the family of the deceased. We are in touch with the family and will provide all support for ensuring the early repatriation of mortal remains.”
In an earlier statement, the embassy said that 11 Indians were among those injured in yesterday’s attack.
Yemen’s Houthis are claiming responsibility for both Saturday and Sunday’s attacks on Riyadh Airport. The group said on Sunday they had targeted Riyadh’s airport several times as well as Saudi energy facilities, a day after Saturday’s deadly attack.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the Iran-backed group “carried out four qualitative operations in the past 24 hours using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones,” AFP reported.
Saree said the group targeted the Riyadh airport multiple times, as well as the Dammam airport and two facilities belonging to the Saudi state oil company Aramco.
Saudi authorities say latest airport attack 'resulted in injuries'
The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement that today’s attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh “resulted in injuries” but did not specify how many.
The statement said that an “assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities is ongoing”.
Earlier on Sunday, an “unidentified projectile” hit Riyadh’s international airport, the same site targeted in Saturday’s strike which injured hundreds of people and killed 12. Minutes earlier, Yemen’s Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack.
Israeli prime minister condemns attack on Riyadh airport
Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, condemned on Sunday the “horrific terrorist attack” on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia.
“I condemn in the strongest possible terms the horrific terrorist attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh,” Netanyahu wrote in a social media post, adding that he extended Israel’s “deepest condolences” to the families of the victims.
Yemen’s Houthis claim responsibility for Riyadh airport attack that killed 12 people
Yemen’s Houthis have claimed responsibility for the attack targeting Riyadh airport, according to a statement released by the group.
The Houthis claimed to have launched strikes against Dammam airport and Saudi Aramco facilities located in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province. It is not immediately clear whether the group is claiming just yesterday’s attack or the strike from earlier today as well. Saudi authorities have not yet issued a confirmation.
SriLankan Airlines announced that it has suspended all flights to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia until October 18 “in view of the recent security incident affecting Riyadh Airport and ongoing safety and operational assessments.”
“The safety and security of our passengers and crew remain our highest priority and services will resume once the prevailing conditions are assessed to be suitable for commercial flight operations,” the statement said.
Attacks on Riyadh airport and capital come on eve of major oil summit
Saudi Arabia of course is the world’s top oil exporter and its oil refineries and facilities have been repeatedly targeted by the Houthis this past month.
It was forced to temporarly close its key East-West pipeline last month after a drone attack on the 1,200km Saudi Aramco pipeline which spans the Arabian peninsula.
That temporarily halted oil flows; the kingdom had been diverting much of its oil that used to go out through the Strait of Hormuz through the pipeline to be shipped out through the Red Sea, however that trade route has now also been targeted by the Iran-allied Houthis.
That has driven up global oil prices and spooked the market. The kingdom was in fact due to host a major oil summit – the World Petroleum Congress - this week in Riyadh.
The CEOs of major companies Shell, ExxonMobil, BP, TotalEnergies had been due to attend but given the attacks, it’s unclear if exceutives will take the risk. Saudi authorities were saying this morning that the summit would still proceed.
If confirmed as a strike, this marks the fourth attack on the Saudi capital’s airport just this week alone.
The Houthis haven’t claimed responsibility for Saturday’s attack on King Khalid International in Riyadh, but earlier this morning issued a threat warning travellers and airlines and trade operators to stay away from all Saudi airports and airspaces – barring those of Islamic holy cities Mecca and Medina.
The Houthis have declared that all Saudi airspace is a theatre of their military operations.
They’ve escalated their attacks as Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of airstrikes on Houthi areas in Yemen this week, as part of the Yemeni government force’s counter-offensive this week to repel the Houthis from a critical Red Sea strait.
Riyadh international airport reportedly hit again in second strike
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen says an “unidentified projectile” hit Riyadh’s international airport on Sunday – the same site targeted in Saturday’s strike which injured hundreds of people and killed 12.
Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Malki said the projectile struck Terminal 4 at King Khalid International Airport, causing a fire, AFP reported.
Al-Malki said air defences also “intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile” in the vicinity of the airport.
The airport has been closed today following yesterday’s deadly attack.
Houthi airport attack forces swift rethink of Trump’s new 'Blame Ukraine' strategy
Patrick Wintour
The reckless missile attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday did not just export the death and misery inside Yemen to Saudi Arabia, it also left Donald Trump forced to reconsider his diplomatic and political strategy designed to take him into the midterm elections next month.
The US president’s plan had only been unveiled on Saturday.
It was to blame what he described as “a world problem” – spiralling diesel prices – on the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, saying his attacks on Russian oil refineries were the cause. He was going to keep the political temperature down on his war of choice in Iran and its spillover in Yemen until after the midterms.
In pursuit of this strategy, he claimed the Iranian blockade in the strait of Hormuz was in effect broken, producing figures on daily oil barrel exports to assuage the markets. As a further insurance he also claimed it was impossible to negotiate with the Iranians since there was no single leadership in Tehran.
Saudi Arabia, in conjunction with Turkey, and Pakistan, were largely to be left to sort out the Houthis along the Red Sea. The fate of Yemen, the poorest country in the world according to the International Monetary Fund, was not going to shift votes in Kansas or Alaska.
Now, after the Riyadh airport attack, it is doubtful, for a basket of reasons, that this anyway threadbare strategy, largely born of desperation, can hold.
For all the talk of the Gulf becoming responsible for its own security, it is doubtful that Saudi Arabia can be left to fend for itself after the carnage in Riyadh. One of the the 12 dead is an American and there may be more among the severely injured. Something is clearly wrong with Saudi defences since the Houthis are firing rockets from 500 miles away, and they are reaching their target too often.
The US has had a unilateral ceasefire with the Houthis since 2025, and once the hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis recommenced in the summer, the pact was quietly renewed.
Trump has twice rejected Saudi appeals for help. Can he spurn them three times? The pressure to act as allies are expected to may prove overwhelming.
Egyptian flight attendant and Syrian woman among 12 killed at Saudi airport
We have some more detail on the 12 people killed in the Houthi missile strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airporton Saturday.
The attack on a civilian space – the airport had no military facility- has drew widespread condemnation from Arab and Western leaders and the UN.
Saudi authorities said the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.
The Egyptian woman killed has been identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, a flight attendant who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to the Egyptian state-run TV.
The Syrian woman has been identified as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida by the Syrian embassy in Riyadh.
She was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for the past five years after fleeing the Syrian civil war, her niece told AP. She had been visiting her sister in Riyadh and was on her way home to Mecca, where she lived, when she was killed in the attack.
There is attention too on the still yet to be identified American citizen who was killed at the airport because that will add to Saudi pressure on Donald Trump for the U.S. to join in the fight.
As we await more detail on this reported blast in the Saudi capital, it’s worth noting that there’s been a distinct lack of information coming from Saudi authorities on the Houthi attacks and other dangers.
Officials have announced that schooling will move online until the end of the week, meaning schools and campuses are closed.
But they have otherwise been largely quiet on the major attack on the country’s largest airport yesterday which killed 12 people and injured 300 more.
They have not issued a wider emergency alert, nor given a national address or offered any assurance to residents on why and how the kingdom’s air defences failed. We know that Saudi Arabia has been requesting more missile interceptors from the US and other European allies – but the US is also facing its own shortage due to the Iran fighting.
The Houthis have targeted Riyadh’s airport for the past few weeks – including two attacks earlier in the week, which killed four people. But Saudi authorities have not publicly announced a closure of King Khalid International Airport, with the suspension of flights detected through air traffic monitoring sites instead.
This withholding of information the public is in line with a pattern of communication from not just Saudi but other Gulf state authorities these past seven months since they’ve come under attack from Iranian missiles and drones.
Gulf authorities have tended to suppress the flow of information – ostensibly for national security purposes and to maintain public confidence in the countr'y’s defences.
However, the lack of information is also leading to confusion and speculation online, particularly as the Houthis continue to threaten new strikes against the kingdom.
Houthi state media says capital's airport hit by Saudi strike
Houthi-run state TV is reporting that Saudia Arabia has carried out a strike on the main airport in Sana’a, the Yemeni capital currently controlled by the Houthis.
Al Masirah TV said the strike had hit Sana’a International Airport.
No comment yet from Saudi authorities or the Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen.
Earlier however, the coalition had issued a issued a statement saying they would “respond decisively” to the Houthis’ “terrorist attack” on Riyadh’s airport on Saturday which killed 12 people and injured 309.
The Saudis have launched hundreds of air strikes on Houthi positions in Yemen since fighting recommenced last month.
UK advises against travel to parts of Saudi Arabia
The UK Foreign Office has updated guidance for British nationals following the deadly Houthi attack on Saturday.
It has advised against:
All travel to within 10km of the border with Yemen
All but essential travel to Aseer province, Riyadh province, Najran province, Jizan province and Taif city and Taif International Airport
There are an estimated 20,000- 30,000 British nationals living in Saudi Arabia, although those numbers have presumably fluctuated since the war began and Iran and its allies fought back against US and Israeli strikes by targeting cities like Dubai and Doha, in Gulf states allied with the US.
In the first fortnight of the war earlier this year in March, more than 102,000 Britons across the Middle East registered with the Foreign Office for help.

articles.title: Trump says Ukraine needs a new president who will agree to end the war
articles.body:
Trump calls on Ukraine to replace Zelenskyy amid tensions over Russia deal
US president suggests Zelenskyy has not done enough to end war as tensions rise over a diesel supply deal with Russia.
United States President Donald Trump has called on Ukraine to replace Volodymyr Zelenskyy, lashing out at the Ukrainian leader for strikes on Russian oil refineries that have contributed to high global diesel prices.
The criticism on Saturday came as tensions between the US and Ukraine have risen after Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Russia.
The steep rise in global fuel prices, which followed the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran, has become a political liability for Trump’s Republican Party as it heads into next month’s midterm elections, in which opposition Democrats could gain control of one or both houses of Congress.
“I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters at the White House, saying Zelenskyy had hurt global diesel supplies with strikes on Russian refineries.
“He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world,” Trump said.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, however, defended Zelenskyy in a post on X.
“He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide,” Sybiha wrote. “Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support.”
Trump, who has been urging Zelenskyy to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure for weeks, struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to reduce high fuel prices.
The deal marked a stunning reversal of years of Washington’s pressure on Russia over its full scale invasion of Ukraine.
Trump has sought to blame record-high US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran.
Mass casualty attacks
The US-Russia deal drew a furious reaction from Zelenskyy, who said it had emboldened Moscow. He linked the agreement with a Russian attack on Saturday that killed 20 people, including three children, in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia.
“Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said.
“Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities,” he said. “Different signals are needed.”
The Zaporizhzhia assault was the third mass-casualty attack on Ukraine in four days.
Nearly 80 civilians were killed in Russian strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, including at least 30 killed by a bomb in the eastern garrison city of Kramatorsk and 22 others by a missile in the town of Pryluky, about 130km (80 miles) east of Kyiv.
Trump’s announcement about the diesel deal was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month aimed at clamping down on Moscow’s oil and gas revenues that fuel the war against Ukraine.
He announced the deal amid talks between Ukrainian and European officials with US negotiators in Miami, Florida, on Friday, which were aimed at developing a common proposal for ending the war, according to the Reuters news agency.
In his remarks at the White House, Trump criticised Zelenskyy over the lack of a peace deal while demanding an end to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities.
“I said to him, ‘Do what you want. Don’t hit refineries. There’s plenty of targets. Don’t hit refineries.’ And he went out and he hit,” Trump said. “He better damn well stop.”
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, but for some reason, he never does,” Trump added.
The diesel deal was criticised by US lawmakers, including one of Trump’s fellow Republicans, Representative Don Bacon, who said it was time to apply more sanctions that Congress had recently passed, not roll them back.
Ukraine’s European allies have also expressed dismay at the Russian deal and said they stood by their commitment to sanctions.
United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke with Zelenskyy on Saturday and said London would strengthen its sanctions on Russia, according to a Downing Street spokesperson.
Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said every additional $1bn Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries and Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine was coordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia will receive and he had spoken to French President Emmanuel Macron about shoring up Ukraine’s air defences.
He went on to warn of an increased risk of further missile strikes in the coming days.
Zelenskyy also said he had discussed the developments with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Ukraine would receive ammunition in the coming days for the F-16 fighter jets used to intercept Russia’s Shahed drones.

articles.title: The Makkah alliance has been called defensive. Now it has to prove it
articles.body:
When Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye signed the Makkah Alliance for Defence in August, most of us read it as a statement of intent. It took barely two months for that to change. On October 5, ministers and commanders met in Riyadh and agreed to activate collective deterrence measures and send forces and capabilities to the Kingdom at speed. The same meeting appointed retired Lt Gen Nauman Mahmood, a Pakistani, as the alliance’s first secretary-general for three years.
Then came Thursday. Two Houthi attacks hit Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, one on the facilities and one on a Saudia aircraft. Three Saudi citizens died, among them a pilot, and people of several nationalities were wounded. Hundreds of flights were cancelled, and European regulators widened their no-fly advisory. By Friday the airport was running normally again. The signal had still been sent: the capital is within reach.
I think this is the moment the alliance has to answer a question it has so far dodged. The pact is modelled on NATO’s Article 5, so an attack on one is treated as an attack on all. Yet all three governments describe it as purely defensive. Both statements can be true only if someone explains where the line sits.
This is not only about Yemen
It helps to remember what kind of war this is. Reuters ties the escalation to the wider US-Iran confrontation. Iranian attacks have choked traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which makes the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait far more valuable than usual. A month ago the Houthis took ground along that coast. Saudi Arabia has answered with a growing air campaign, Sanaa included, and Yemeni government forces backed by Riyadh have launched a large offensive that their government says is meant to retake everything the Houthis have conquered. The coalition says it hit 324 targets and gave those forces air cover.
So the state this alliance is rushing to protect is also a state on the attack. That does not make Saudi Arabia’s position illegitimate, because it is being struck hard. But it does mean “defensive” cannot be assumed. It has to be shown.
Where the language starts to strain
Prince Khalid bin Salman said the committee would act against the attacks and “all those responsible for them”. I keep coming back to that phrase. It could mean the Houthis. It could mean their sponsors. The statement does not say.
Islamabad has been more careful. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif says Pakistani and Turkish forces are in a supportive role while only Saudi troops fight, and he has described that support as including reconnaissance. His test for the pact to apply is unprovoked aggression or spillover from Yemen into Saudi territory, which is a fair standard. And on October 9 the Foreign Office spokesman said allied forces would not attack from or inside Yemen, dismissing reports of Pakistani strikes as speculation.
I take those statements at face value. Nothing in the public record puts Pakistani or Turkish soldiers in combat in Yemen. But “supportive” covers a lot of ground, and some of the reporting is awkward. Middle East Eye, citing Reuters, says Pakistan flew four plane loads of weapons to Aden for the Saudi-backed government. I could not find any official Pakistani confirmation, so that stays an unverified report for now. If it is accurate, though, it is hard to square with the Foreign Office line. Guarding Saudi cities from missiles is one thing. Arming one side of a ground offensive is another, and people in Pakistan are entitled to know which one their country is doing.
How many troops, exactly?
The numbers in circulation come from reporters, not from the government. In May, Reuters reported that Pakistan had sent 8,000 troops, a fighter squadron and an air-defence system. On October 2 it quoted a Pakistani official saying 30,000 to 40,000 troops were helping guard Saudi land borders and intercept drones and missiles.
The army’s spokesman has now confirmed that Pakistani forces are in the Kingdom in “multiple capabilities and domains” and have been for decades. That is accurate, and it is also a little convenient. A decades-old training and advisory mission is a very different thing from a force of tens of thousands on border defence. Nobody in government has told the public which description fits.
I understand why troop positions are kept quiet. Revealing them can get people killed. But the overall size, purpose and limits of a commitment this large are a matter of public policy, and they should not be treated as an operational secret.
READ: Turkiye completes preparations to submit Mecca defense pact to parliament: Foreign minister
Ankara has not finished its homework
The pact brings together NATO’s second-largest army, the Muslim world’s only nuclear-armed state and the leading Gulf power. On paper that is formidable. In practice, the three are not at the same stage. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said Turkiye is still assessing how it can help, and the Turkish parliament has not ratified the agreement. Reports say the government plans to take it to parliament, which would clear the way for a deployment. Until that happens, Ankara’s role rests on executive decisions alone, and a pact that lacks legislative backing at home will be hard to sustain once casualties rise.
Pakistan’s difficult position
Pakistan has the most to balance. Years ago its parliament voted unanimously against sending combat troops into the Yemen conflict, and nobody has formally revoked that stance. Pakistan also has a long border with Iran, which supports the Houthis, and a large Shia community at home. Any sense that the country is slipping from defence into offence would carry costs inside Pakistan as well as abroad.
And Islamabad is not short of other worries. India on the eastern frontier, Afghanistan on the western one, and militancy in Balochistan all take up men and money. The economy is fragile, too. A new $1.2 billion IMF deal comes with a warning that the Middle East conflict is weighing on growth, and the families who depend on Gulf remittances feel every escalation directly.
None of this is an argument for walking away from Riyadh. The bond is old and deep, built on faith, history and shared interest. It is an argument for a commitment that Pakistan can actually carry.
On adding new members
People keep asking whether other Muslim countries will join. The Foreign Office has said expansion is “not on the cards” at the moment. I read that as a pause, not a refusal. A bigger alliance is not automatically a stronger one, since every new member brings its own threat perceptions and its own limits on using force. The pause is reasonable, but only if the three founders can make their own arrangement work first.
Defence is not the same as victory
Say the air defences work perfectly. Yemen’s war would still be there. Missiles can be shot down, but the political, territorial and sectarian quarrels behind this conflict will not be solved by interceptors. The danger is a slow slide: an alliance created to protect civilians gradually becomes responsible for a campaign with no clear end. That slide is most likely if Saudi offensive goals, like taking back the Red Sea coast, start to be treated as the alliance’s own.
What I would ask of the alliance
I would start with three things. First, publish a short statement of what the alliance defends, what triggers collective action and what it will never do. It should cover cross-border operations and arms supplied to forces inside Yemen. Second, brief the legislatures. Pakistan’s parliament should hear in closed session what the troop levels and rules of engagement are, and Turkiye should finish its ratification. Third, say plainly that all this military readiness is meant to bring about talks, and back that with real work through Oman, the UN and regional partners alongside it.
How we will know
The alliance began with the promise that regional powers can look after their own security. Thursday’s attack shows how badly that is needed. But I will not judge it by troop numbers or by how many flags appear at the next meeting. I will watch whether Riyadh’s airports stay open, whether civilians are safer, whether the war stays contained, and whether the governments involved can tell their own citizens, honestly, what they have signed up for.
If they can, this could become a template for regional cooperation. If they cannot, it will be remembered as an alliance that promised more than it defined.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia can fight the Houthis, it may not be able to defeat them
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia can afford a long war. It can buy aircraft, missiles, drones, air-defense systems and intelligence. It can absorb losses that would bankrupt a poorer state. Yet that does not mean it can defeat the Houthis. That distinction has become impossible to ignore. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman reportedly called Donald Trump twice last week and urged Washington to strike the Houthis directly. Trump declined, although Washington agreed to provide intelligence and targeting support. The episode is revealing not because Saudi Arabia lacks military power, but because Riyadh appears to recognize that the Houthi problem is no longer one that firepower alone can solve.
The timing matters. The Houthis have seized Mocha on Yemen’s Red Sea coast and moved toward strategically important islands at the mouth of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. At the same time, attacks attributed to Iran-aligned forces have disrupted Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, the very infrastructure designed to give Riyadh an alternative route around the Strait of Hormuz. This leaves Saudi Arabia facing a strategic problem that is much harder than defeating an insurgency. It must protect an economic system built around a handful of extraordinarily valuable and geographically exposed nodes. The Houthis do not need to conquer Saudi Arabia. They only need to make Saudi Arabia’s critical infrastructure sufficiently vulnerable, costly and unpredictable.
Saudi Has the Firepower
On paper, the balance is overwhelmingly in Saudi Arabia’s favor. Riyadh spent an estimated $83.2 billion on its military in 2025, making it the world’s eighth-largest military spender. It possesses advanced fighter aircraft, precision weapons, sophisticated air defenses and extensive access to Western intelligence and technology. The Houthis, by comparison, are a much poorer non-state actor operating from one of the Middle East’s most difficult physical environments. Yet the conventional balance has never translated into decisive strategic victory.
Saudi Arabia entered Yemen’s war in 2015 with overwhelming airpower and a clear political objective: prevent the Houthis from consolidating control over Yemen and restore a government friendly to Riyadh. Years of airstrikes imposed enormous damage and slowed Houthi advances, but they did not produce the political outcome Saudi Arabia wanted.
The lesson is that airpower is poorly suited to solving a political problem when the adversary can disperse, regenerate and operate below the threshold of conventional war. The Houthis have spent the past decade adapting precisely to that imbalance. According to ACLED, they conducted nearly 1,000 rocket and missile attacks and more than 350 distinct drone attacks against Saudi and Emirati territory between 2015 and the April 2022 truce. More importantly, the character of those attacks changed. Guided missiles accounted for just 15 percent of Houthi rocket and missile events in 2015, but 89 percent by 2022. Drone attacks also increasingly outnumbered missile attacks.
That evolution points to a fundamental strategic mismatch. Saudi Arabia has generally sought to punish the Houthis by destroying military assets and degrading their operational capacity. The Houthis, meanwhile, have increasingly sought to deny Saudi Arabia the ability to operate securely and predictably. That is the difference between punishment and denial. A military power can destroy a missile launcher. It cannot easily destroy the political and economic incentives behind a dispersed missile force. It can intercept a drone. It cannot guarantee that the next drone will not find another vulnerability. It can strike a command center. It cannot bomb away the geography that gives an adversary access to a strategic maritime chokepoint.
The 2019 attack on Abqaiq and Khurais illustrated the problem dramatically. The assault temporarily knocked out more than half of Saudi oil production and almost 5 percent of global oil supply.
Whether the attack was launched from Iranian or Iraqi territory or claimed by the Houthis, its strategic lesson was unmistakable that a relatively inexpensive asymmetric attack could impose enormous costs on one of the world’s most heavily armed states. That is why Saudi Arabia’s military superiority should not be confused with strategic invulnerability.
The Houthis Are No Longer Fighting Only for Yemen
The most important change in 2026 is that the Houthi threat is no longer primarily territorial. It is increasingly geographic and economic. The seizure of Mocha and the Houthi advance toward Perim Island and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait have altered the strategic map. Bab al-Mandeb is not simply another battlefield. It is one of the world’s principal maritime chokepoints, linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. Reuters reported that Houthi forces reached the strategic island of Perim on September 11, putting them closer to the maritime gateway through which energy and commercial traffic moves between the Middle East, Europe and Asia.
READ: Saudi Arabia says 3 killed in attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid airport
That development matters enormously for Saudi Arabia. For years, Riyadh has invested in reducing its dependence on the Strait of Hormuz. The East-West Pipeline is central to that strategy because it allows Saudi crude to reach the Red Sea port of Yanbu without passing through Hormuz. But the geography of the current conflict is beginning to turn that strategy against Riyadh. Hormuz is under pressure from Iran. Bab al-Mandeb is increasingly exposed to the Houthis. And the East-West Pipeline has itself been disrupted by drone attacks attributed to Iran-aligned forces in Iraq. Reuters reported that the pipeline outage could threaten as much as 4 percent of global oil supply, while Saudi crude production had already fallen sharply from earlier levels.
This is no longer a conventional war in the familiar sense. It is a contest over the reliability of economic geography. That distinction is critical.
Iran and its aligned forces do not need to seize Saudi oil fields. They do not even need to shut down every shipping lane. They only need to increase the risk attached to the routes through which Saudi energy reaches the global market. This is chokepoint warfare. The objective is not necessarily to control every inch of territory. It is to acquire leverage over the narrow points through which enormous volumes of trade must pass.
That is precisely why Houthi capabilities matter beyond Yemen. ACLED has documented how the group previously used drones and missiles against airports and hydrocarbon facilities rather than concentrating solely on battlefield targets. From 2018 to early 2022, 43 percent of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia targeted civilian airports and energy infrastructure. The logic is brutally efficient that attack what the adversary cannot afford to lose. For Saudi Arabia, that means oil infrastructure, ports, pipelines, airports and increasingly maritime routes. The Houthis therefore do not have to win a conventional war. They only have to make the cost of maintaining normality rise faster than Riyadh’s ability or willingness to absorb it.
Can Saudi Afford to Defeat Houthis?
This is where the question of Saudi military capability becomes inseparable from the question of Saudi economic strategy. Riyadh can certainly retaliate. It can intensify airstrikes, deploy more intelligence assets, expand missile defenses and work with regional partners. Saudi Arabia has enough resources to impose substantial costs on the Houthis. The harder question is whether escalation would actually solve the problem. A heavier Saudi campaign could force the Houthis underground. It could destroy launch sites and command infrastructure. But it could also generate the very response Riyadh wants to avoid: more attacks against oil facilities, cities, ports and shipping. That is the escalation paradox.
If Saudi Arabia restrains itself, the Houthis may consolidate their position around Bab al-Mandeb and strengthen their bargaining power. If Saudi Arabia escalates dramatically, the Houthis may retaliate against the infrastructure that makes Saudi Arabia economically powerful but strategically exposed. The request to Trump therefore makes more sense in this context. MBS was not necessarily asking Washington to fight Saudi Arabia’s war for it. He was seeking to alter the cost-benefit equation by adding American military power to the deterrence equation. Trump’s refusal to authorize direct strikes, while allowing intelligence and targeting support, exposes a new strategic reality that Riyadh cannot automatically assume that Washington will absorb the escalation risks associated with every Saudi security problem.
That leaves Saudi Arabia with a difficult choice. It can fight the Houthis alone. But a war of indefinite containment would consume resources and expose critical infrastructure. A campaign designed to achieve decisive victory could be even more dangerous because it would invite retaliation against precisely those assets Saudi Arabia is trying to protect. The central problem, therefore, is not Saudi Arabia’s military weakness. It is Saudi Arabia’s strategic exposure. The Houthis possess less firepower, less money and fewer sophisticated weapons. Yet they can exploit a fundamental asymmetry, the cost of launching an attack can be tiny compared with the cost of defending every potential target.
A cheap drone can force the deployment of expensive interceptors. A single strike on a pipeline can disrupt millions of barrels of potential exports. A credible threat to shipping can raise insurance premiums even without sinking a single tanker. A temporary closure of a chokepoint can create economic consequences far beyond the battlefield. This is why the Houthi challenge should not be measured by the territory the group controls or the number of weapons it possesses. It should be measured by the amount of strategic uncertainty it can impose.
Saudi Arabia therefore faces a paradox that extends far beyond Yemen. It has sufficient military power to fight the Houthis, but military superiority does not guarantee strategic immunity. Riyadh can degrade the group, deter some attacks and impose painful costs. What it cannot easily do is eliminate the geography, economic exposure and asymmetric incentives that make the Houthi strategy possible.
That is the real lesson of the current crisis. Saudi Arabia does not need to become militarily stronger simply to defeat the Houthis. It needs to become strategically harder to coerce. That means diversifying energy routes, hardening critical infrastructure, improving integrated air and missile defense, strengthening maritime security, expanding regional intelligence cooperation and, above all, reducing the number of single points of failure on which its economic model depends. The Houthis have exposed a vulnerability that money and military technology alone cannot solve. Saudi Arabia can win battles against them. But unless Riyadh changes the strategic geometry of the contest, the Houthis may not need to win the war.

Russia’s Ballistic Attack on Kyiv Shows the Real Cost of Trump-Putin Diesel Deal, Zelenskyy Says
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the Trump-Putin diesel deal after Russia launched a daytime ballistic missile attack on Kyiv on October 10, warning that allowing Moscow to earn more from petroleum exports would fuel further Russian attacks on Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In a statement on October 10, Zelenskyy said Russian forces launched ballistic missiles at Kyiv following repeated attacks by jet-powered Shahed drones against Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Ukrainian air defenses managed to intercept some of the incoming missiles.
“What allowing Russia to sell petroleum products means was heard most clearly in Kyiv today,” Zelenskyy said, warning that Moscow intends to continue its war, terrorize civilians, and destroy infrastructure.
According to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko on October 10, a Russian missile struck a restaurant building in the capital’s Obolonskyi district, sparking a fire and injuring four people, one of whom was in serious condition.
At another location in the same district, missile debris fell into the courtyard of a residential building.
Ukraine’s Air Force had warned of multiple missiles heading toward Kyiv shortly before explosions rocked the capital. Local reports described three to four explosions during the attack, while Ukrainian air defenses engaged incoming threats.
Zelenskyy warned that additional Russian oil revenues would directly finance Moscow’s military operations.
“Every additional billion dollars they can earn from exports will be spent precisely on this,” he said, referring to the purchase of critical components, weapons-production equipment, upgraded Shahed drones, missiles, and additional troops.
“Russia’s choice is war,” Zelenskyy declared, adding that Moscow would only be prepared to stop fighting once its ability to prolong the invasion was reduced. He called for stronger action from Washington, Europe, and other international partners to support Ukraine and restrict Russia’s ability to wage war.
The remarks followed Trump’s October 9 announcement of a diesel supply agreement with Putin, under which Russia would deliver petroleum products to the United States and global markets.
Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, with additional shipments planned afterward. The US Treasury also issued a temporary license easing sanctions on Russian diesel exports.

articles.title: Ukraine Ready to Halt Refinery Strikes for Energy Truce, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Sunday, Oct. 11, that Ukraine is prepared to halt long-range strikes against Russian oil refineries if Russia ceases attacks against Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
In a statement on Facebook reviewing weekly Russian aerial bombardments, Zelensky said halting attacks on power and utility networks is achievable immediately, but asserted that Moscow remains unwilling to de-escalate.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“It is feasible to stop strikes on energy today, but [Russian President Vladimir] Putin does not want to do this,” Zelensky stated.
“Ukraine will be ready to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries if Russia ceases strikes against our energy infrastructure. Any de-escalation steps must be mutual and with real guarantees.”
Zelensky emphasized that Russia bears sole responsibility for the war in Europe, noting that diplomatic engagements with European leaders are scheduled throughout Sunday to coordinate additional defense packages, primarily surface-to-air defense systems and ammunition for combat aviation.
Weekly strike toll and escalating civilian casualties
Zelensky highlighted the operational scale of Russian standoff strikes over the preceding seven days, reporting that Russian forces launched approximately 1,450 guided aerial bombs (KABs), 75 missiles of various types, and more than 1,640 strike drones against Ukrainian territory.
According to the president, roughly 60 percent of the unmanned aerial vehicles deployed during the weekly barrages were high-speed, turbojet-powered variants engineered to challenge low-altitude air defense interception networks.
Zaporizhzhia Bombing Death Toll Reaches 20 as Rescue Ends
The weekly barrage produced casualties and structural destruction across multiple provinces.
Zelensky confirmed that search and rescue operations in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia concluded on Sunday morning following a Russian guided bomb strike on a residential apartment building, with the final death toll rising to 23, including four children.
In the Kharkiv region, Russian munitions struck a healthcare facility on Saturday, while overnight attacks engaged municipal civilian infrastructure, residential housing, and regional utility grids.
“I am grateful to all our emergency services, who are always alongside our people and resolving consequences after Russian strikes,” Zelensky said.
Petrochemical targeting and the energy armistice framework
Zelensky’s proposal for a reciprocal cessation of energy attacks comes amid an intensified Ukrainian interdiction campaign directed against downstream petrochemical logistics across the Russian Federation.
Overnight into Saturday, Oct. 10, Ukrainian Defense Forces conducted a repeat strike against the Samara linear production and dispatching station (LVDS) near Prosvet in Russia’s Samara region.
The critical petrochemical junction blends petroleum streams to formulate standardized export-grade Urals crude while supplying refined petroleum products to the Russian armed forces.
The attack followed an earlier precision strike on Oct. 7 that destroyed four large-capacity RVS-50000 crude oil storage reservoirs at the facility.
The interdiction of refining and transshipment nodes forms part of a wider asymmetric campaign that has also engaged deep logistical facilities, including the Yug Rusi oil terminal in Rostov-on-Don and multiple corporate data centers in Vladimir, Kaluga, and Ryazan regions.
The issue of refinery strikes has emerged as a central point of friction between Kyiv and Washington.
US officials have urged Ukraine to unilaterally halt drone strikes on Russian refining capacity to mitigate pressure on international fuel benchmarks, a request that coincided with a controversial bilateral agreement between US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin to permit Russian diesel exports onto global markets.
Ukrainian officials have consistently rejected calls for unilateral restraint, arguing that degrading Russian refining infrastructure directly restricts fuel supplies to frontline Russian military units and diminishes state revenues supporting Moscow’s war effort.
Zelensky reiterated that a suspension of deep interdiction operations can occur only within the framework of an enforceable, bilateral agreement that shields Ukraine’s domestic power and heating grid ahead of the winter season.
