articles.title: Iran at the threshold, Israel outside the room - opinion
articles.body:
One justification for war with Iran was that time was running out. Tehran, Israelis were told, was “racing” toward nuclear weapons, “a step away” from a bomb.
Yet Iran has been near the nuclear threshold for years. Its distance from a weapon has never depended solely on centrifuges, enriched uranium, or the time needed to produce fissile material. US intelligence assessed that Tehran had acquired capabilities bringing it close to the threshold but had not decided to cross it. A crucial barrier was political.
Six months into the war, it is difficult to say that barrier has strengthened. Nuclear facilities have been damaged, but subsequent US intelligence assessments do not indicate a significant increase in the time Iran would need to produce a weapon.
Questions remain about its enriched uranium stockpile, while discussion in Iran about crossing the threshold has become more open. The war has also opened a front in the Strait of Hormuz and increased Israel’s diplomatic costs, particularly in the United States. Whether it has made Israel safer from nuclear threats remains unclear.
The only effort in the past decade that successfully imposed agreed, monitored, verifiable limits on Iran’s nuclear program was diplomatic. The 2015 agreement dramatically reduced its enriched uranium stockpile, restricted enrichment and centrifuges, and introduced extensive monitoring.
The International Atomic Energy Agency and Western intelligence assessments found Iran compliant with its core nuclear commitments. Missiles, proxies, and other security issues could – and still can – be addressed separately.
When the Trump administration withdrew unilaterally in May 2018 and reimposed sanctions, the IAEA was still verifying compliance. Iran began exceeding the limits afterward. Israel’s push for US withdrawal, followed by the shift from diplomacy to war, demands a sober assessment of this strategy’s costs.
A low-risk diplomatic option remains largely unknown to Israelis. Since 2019, regional states have gathered annually at UN headquarters in New York for the Conference on the Establishment of a Middle East Zone Free of Nuclear Weapons and Other Weapons of Mass Destruction. Its seventh session takes place this November. Iran and the Arab states participate. Israel is invited but stays away.
Israel has long argued that disarmament cannot be separated from regional security; that arrangements must be developed by regional states with their consent; and that states cannot relinquish capabilities considered essential while remaining in conflict with their neighbors.
It has rightly opposed focusing exclusively on its nuclear capabilities while ignoring missiles, chemical and biological weapons, and other threats. These concerns remain relevant.
They do not, however, require postponing disarmament discussions until peace, recognition, normalization, and extensive confidence-building measures have been achieved. Arab states see this approach as an endless series of prerequisites before weapons of mass destruction reach the table.
Peace, confidence-building, arms control, and disarmament can advance in parallel. War only increases the need for communication, escalation prevention, monitoring, and agreements.
Changing the regional landscape
Participation in November would not require Israel to relinquish weapons attributed to it, join the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), abandon nuclear ambiguity, or accept a future treaty in advance. The conference operates by consensus: regional states participate, and decisions cannot be imposed on Israel.
Several longstanding Israeli demands are therefore already met. If Israel wants missiles, delivery systems, escalation prevention, regional security, and confidence-building on the agenda, it should make those demands inside the room.
Participation could itself build mutual confidence. Israel would discuss weapons of mass destruction directly with its neighbors without committing to an outcome. Arab states and Iran would have to accept Israel as a full, equal negotiating partner.
This would not constitute normalization: states conditioning full relations on ending the occupation and reaching an Israeli-Palestinian settlement could retain their positions. But accepting Israel as a legitimate participant would matter to a country that has long insisted recognition and regional relations are essential to disarmament.
The United States also stays away. Alongside its own reservations, Washington has linked its absence to incomplete regional participation and Israel’s opposition to the format.
An Israeli shift could enable an American one. The government formed after October’s elections could invite Washington to join it in November. After months of confrontation with Iran, this would be a significant diplomatic gesture without advance commitments to disarmament, NPT accession, or an unwritten treaty.
There are precedents. Israel participated in Arms Control and Regional Security talks with Arab states in the 1990s and consultations on a weapons of mass destruction conference in 2013–2014; Iran attended one meeting.
Beginning in 1980, Israel joined the UN General Assembly consensus supporting a nuclear-weapon-free Middle East for over two decades, while retaining reservations about how to achieve it. Attending November’s conference would revive a tradition of raising objections and demanding conditions while continuing to talk.
Meanwhile, the regional landscape is changing. Saudi Arabia is expanding its civilian nuclear program and security alliances, including the Mecca Agreement with Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan. Iran is reconsidering its nuclear future, and another confrontation remains possible.
Burying one’s nuclear head in the sand does not preserve freedom of action. It leaves others free to shape the reality Israel must confront.
The next government should arrive in New York with Israel’s security interests, reservations, demands, and proposals – and ask Washington to join it. It need not commit to disarmament. Entering the room does not endanger Israel’s security. In today’s regional reality, remaining outside requires an explanation.
The writer is a guest writer at the Mitvim Institute and an advocate for eliminating nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction from the Middle East. She is the founder and executive director of the Middle East Treaty Organization (METO).

articles.title: Midterm panic pushes Trump to trade Zelensky for cheaper diesel
articles.body:
Midterm panic pushes Trump to trade Zelensky for cheaper diesel
TEHRAN — With the 2026 U.S. midterm elections a month away and diesel at $6.28 a gallon, Donald Trump went looking for someone to blame and settled on Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky, whose official presidential mandate expired long ago and whose continued rule under suspended elections remains constitutionally questionable.
On Friday, after talks with Vladimir Putin, Trump announced that Russia would ship more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, 500,000 in November and a million after that.
U.S. Treasury’s General License 135 makes it legal, reportedly until April 7, 2027. Trump signed a Russia sanctions law last month. He thanked Putin anyway.
The fuel crunch traces to the war on Iran, which the United States and Israel opened on February 28 and which has throttled Persian Gulf supply since. Trump blames Ukrainian drones hitting Russian refineries instead. Analysts are unconvinced.
Analyst Tom Kloza called the announcement “more noise from Truth Social,” adding that Ukrainian drones have reportedly crippled about half of Russia’s refining. Ed Hirs of the University of Houston told Newsweek that he expects relief at the pump only well after the election, and only a temporary one, because the pledged volume is small next to the global market.
Saturday brought the insult. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters, accusing Zelensky of wanting “to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel.”
The same day, Russian glide bombs reportedly hit Zaporizhzhia, where Ukrainian officials counted at least 21 dead, three of them children. Zelensky called Washington’s waiver “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.”
The timing was almost comic. Ukrainian and European officials were in Miami with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner when the announcement landed, and a senior Ukrainian official told the AP that Kyiv had no warning.
A U.S. official gave Axios another version: Trump moved after Zelensky ignored roughly six requests to stop hitting Russian refineries. Ukrainian officials say Washington threatened to cut intelligence sharing.
Sunday’s Truth Social post claimed an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE,” effective immediately. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Zelensky said the announcement “was news for me,” and said Ukraine will comply if Moscow does.
Trump tried this on September 14. Neither capital confirmed it then, and both kept striking each other’s energy sites.
The pattern is hard to miss. Washington announces by social media post, informs its partner afterward and calls the result a deal.
Kyiv is asked to stop hitting refineries, absorb strikes on its power grid and, if Trump gets his way, hold an election under bombardment. Moscow may get sanctions relief and export revenue. Stockholm and Berlin claimed they are keeping their sanctions, even if Washington is not.

articles.title: Once considered “taboo,” Russian assassination plots against European defense executives are escalating as its hybrid warfare grows bolder, intelligence agencies warn – FT
articles.body:
Russia is expanding efforts to target European defense industry leaders as part of a broader campaign of sabotage and hybrid operations aimed at weakening support for Ukraine, the Financial Times reported on 11 October, citing officials from five European intelligence agencies.
The warnings come amid a wider increase in Russia-linked sabotage and other covert operations targeting European defense companies and critical infrastructure. Moscow is expanding its so-called hybrid warfare campaign against European countries as they continue to support Ukraine, using covert networks, intimidation, and suspected sabotage to undermine security and deter further assistance to Kyiv.
The FT reported that assassinations of civilian targets in Europe, once considered "taboo" even within Russian intelligence services, are becoming an increasingly prominent part of the Kremlin’s plans.
Russian operatives target defense industry leaders
European intelligence officials told the FT that Russian operatives are targeting chief executives and senior employees at defense companies, including smaller firms manufacturing drones and drone components.
The campaign comes as Russia seeks to undermine European backing for Ukraine amid a battlefield stalemate and mounting pressure on the Russian economy.
The warnings have prompted defense companies to strengthen security around senior executives. Some have increased personal protection, while others have relocated production sites in response to suspected Russian threats, according to the FT.
Germany's domestic intelligence service, the BfV, has stepped up contact with employees and management at German defense companies and recommended that some use privately contracted close-protection teams, an agency official told the newspaper.
BfV chief Sinan Selen warned German lawmakers that Russia was deliberately planning acts of violence against individuals through state or state-controlled actors. He said the operations were evolving in their targets, methods, and use of organized crime networks.
Russia adapts its methods to carry out attacks
According to the intelligence officials cited by the FT, Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, has adapted its methods by working more closely with criminal groups and dividing surveillance, logistics, planning, and execution among different operatives.
Officials said some plots had been disrupted, while other cases involved surveillance of targets at home and at work.
The campaign's intended effect extends beyond any individual attack. One European intelligence official told the FT that the threat is psychological, designed to make people reconsider doing business with Ukraine.
Although some Russian operations remain amateurish and have been detected early, the resulting uncertainty forces companies to devote more resources to security. Smaller firms, which may have fewer resources to protect their personnel and facilities, could be particularly vulnerable.
Plot against Rheinmetall CEO raised alarm in 2024
European defense executives have been on heightened alert since 2024, when US and German intelligence agencies uncovered a Russian plot against Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger, a prominent advocate of supplying weapons to Ukraine.
Papperger has said he now receives round-the-clock protection from private security personnel and police.
The FT reported that European intelligence agencies now view threats against defense industry leaders as part of a broader effort to disrupt the production and supply of weapons to Ukraine, rather than isolated plots against individual executives.

articles.title: Trump declares immediate energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. Zelenskyy says it was news to him, but Ukraine’s ready
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has announced an immediate energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine, saying both sides agreed to stop striking each other’s energy facilities, in a post on Truth Social. Ukraine, however, knew nothing about the deal.
Russia has spent the war hitting Ukraine's power plants, refineries, and grids, while Ukraine answered with strikes on its refineries and plants that produce missiles. If confirmed, a halt before winter would be a major break. Yet about seven minutes before Trump’s announcement, Russia struck at Kyiv’s thermal plant, cutting power to several districts of the capital at once.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote.
News for Zelenskyy
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Axios the announcement “was news" for him. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree, he added. Moscow gave no immediate confirmation.
The announcement follows days of friction over energy. Washington has just eased sanctions on Russian diesel and pressed Kyiv to stop hitting Russian refineries, while Russian strikes killed more than 80 Ukrainian civilians in two days.
A truce no one in Kyiv confirmed
Zelenskyy had already signaled Ukraine’s terms. He said on Sunday that Kyiv was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted its attacks on Ukrainian energy, so the condition was on the table before Trump spoke, not settled by him.
If Trump negotiated it with Putin, then he should say when the ceasefire begins, Zelenskyy added, underlining that Ukraine had not been party to any such agreement.
Ukrainians greet it with doubt
The reaction in Kyiv was wary. Trump already declared an energy ceasefire once, and Putin broke it within five minutes, said Andrii Kovalenko, former head of Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, asking whether Trump was now “announcing it to himself.”
Meanwhile, lawmaker Yaroslav Zhelezniak called for an explanation, warning that Trump’s “energy ceasefire” might mean Ukraine stops hitting Russian refineries and tankers while Russia merely promises not to strike Ukrainian oil tankers it would struggle to find in the first place.

articles.title: Trump claims Russia and Ukraine have agreed to stop attacks on energy infrastructure
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacks on each other's energy infrastructure with immediate effect. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the announcement had come as a surprise but expressed support for the proposal, while Moscow had yet to confirm any agreement.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, without providing details about the terms or implementation.
Zelenskyy initially told Axios that the announcement "was news for me", adding that Ukraine would accept a halt to energy attacks if Russia agreed to the same conditions.
He subsequently confirmed Kyiv's support in a statement on X, saying Ukraine was awaiting information from Washington.
"Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it's important for Russia to support it as well," he wrote.
Zelenskyy said he had discussed the proposal with Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
The announcement followed days of disagreements between Washington and Kyiv after Trump agreed on Friday to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports in exchange for fuel supplies.
Under the arrangement, Russia would supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to American and international markets.
Trump has linked Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries to rising diesel prices in the United States, where his Republican Party faces congressional elections in November.
Zelenskyy criticised the agreement, warning that additional energy revenues would help Moscow finance its military operations.
Trump responded on Saturday by urging Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries and suggesting the country needed a different president.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal," Trump told reporters.
Speaking to ABC News on Sunday, Zelenskyy rejected outside pressure over Ukraine's leadership but said he would organise elections if Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.
"Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organise elections," he said.
Ukrainian law prohibits elections under martial law, which has remained in force since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The Ukrainian president also reiterated that Kyiv would suspend strikes against Russian oil refineries if Moscow stopped attacking Ukrainian electricity and heating infrastructure.
Russian strikes continued over the weekend, causing casualties and power outages in several Ukrainian regions.
Ukrainian officials reported at least 20 deaths in Saturday's attacks on Zaporizhzhia, including children. Six people were injured in overnight strikes on the Dnipropetrovsk region, according to Ukraine's emergency services.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian drones struck a Yandex data centre in Vladimir, east of Moscow, on Sunday, forcing the Russian technology company to suspend operations at the facility.
The BBC reported that the incident marked the third attack on Yandex infrastructure within a week, following strikes in Sasovo and Kaluga.
The company reported disruptions to several services but said nobody was injured in Sunday's attack.
European officials criticised Washington's decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that the agreement would provide Moscow with additional revenue for its war. She said EU foreign ministers planned to consider sanctions targeting approximately 1,600 individuals and organisations on Monday.
Trump previously announced an energy ceasefire in September, but neither Russia nor Ukraine subsequently confirmed an agreement, and attacks continued.

articles.title: Iran is at the breaking point – the regime’s greatest fear is what comes next - opinion
articles.body:
A nation of 90 million is watching its homeland being impoverished, terrorized, plundered, and driven toward the abyss by a ruling cult that would sooner destroy Iran than relinquish power.
For nearly half a century, the Islamic Republic has consumed the country it claims to govern – its wealth, dignity, security, and the hopes of generations. Now, as economic collapse, repression and the specter of war converge, Iran is approaching a historic breaking point: Will the regime that has held it captive since 1979 finally fall – or drag the country into the abyss with it?
Iran is engulfed in chaos, its economy already collapsing. An incompetent government, presided over by a subservient and populist president, convenes emergency meetings as the country descends deeper into crisis.
Yet Iranians no longer heed the regime’s deceptive promises. The government has lost its grip on the economy and inflation, while Tehran’s markets spiral into turmoil. Officials’ hollow pronouncements and empty assurances no longer command the slightest credibility.
Only the regime’s loyalists profit from the status quo, prepared to watch Iran be destroyed for their financial interests. This same circle has pillaged the country from end to end. Poverty and relentless inflation have brought Iran to its knees.
Iran’s regime prepares for a broader war
Since 1979, a criminal cult has ravaged, plundered, and suppressed the country in service of a fraudulent ideology, holding 90 million people captive. Its rulers now proclaim themselves “the superpower of the world,” boast of having “defeated America and Israel,” and warn that “the region will not be safe as long as even one American soldier remains in the Middle East.”
From state media to Friday-prayer pulpits, regime platforms threaten US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while Islamic murderers and criminals relentlessly inflame hostility toward Israel and the United States.
The Islamic Republic is preparing for a broader war and has no desire for an agreement with Trump. Through deception and duplicity, it keeps him entangled in diplomacy and proclaims that deception a victory. The regime will not hand Trump the political triumph of an agreement, even at the price of every Iranian’s life and Iran itself reduced to scorched earth.
Iran’s military and security establishment remains committed to warmongering and crisis-making. Trump says Washington does not know whom to talk to in Iran. Then what purpose is served by this hollow theater of negotiations with Islamic murderers and terrorists? Six years of his presidency have pursued this impossible dream without producing a single signed agreement.
Meanwhile, Iranians live with profound insecurity, despair, and abandonment. Executions, torture, arrests, and persecution have become grim fixtures of ordinary life. The struggle for basic subsistence has left society paralyzed, angry, and exhausted. While ordinary citizens are denied prosperity and opportunity, money continues flowing to notorious religious institutions, the shadowy Shi’ite clerical mafia, the machinery of repression, and the regime’s vast propaganda apparatus.
The regime is releasing criminals from prison, arming them with swords, knives, and sledgehammers, and unleashing them to threaten Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, the only alternative and leader of Iran’s national uprising – including explicit threats against his life.
Alongside the regime stands a jealous, ambitious, and self-aggrandizing opposition: religious-nationalists, reformists, communists, Kurdish separatists (KDPI, Komala), anti-Israel and anti-American terrorists such as the Mujahedin-e Khalq (MEK), discredited human-rights activists, and mercenaries. Much of this opposition acts in concert, little more than puppets performing before cameras.
In the event of an American and Israeli attack, the regime intends to drag Iran into civil war and reactivate Islamic terrorist networks through the mosques. Its organic relationship with al-Qaeda and ISIS is becoming increasingly unmistakable, while Iran’s borders remain open to them. Hashd al-Shaabi, the Fatemiyoun, the Zainabiyoun, and others are integral components of the Islamic Republic’s machinery of repression.
The regime’s propaganda apparatus promotes weapons training, as though a regime nearing collapse is preparing its supporters for urban warfare. Under the banner of confronting America and Israel, it provides military training with an unmistakable objective: to bring war into Iran’s cities, streets, and alleyways. Islamic terrorists know neither peace nor the value of life and security.
Across Iranian cities, the atmosphere is increasingly one of war. People whisper: Will Trump launch the final attack? The country hangs like a pendulum in uncertainty, with law and order unraveling. The mullahs intensify street propaganda to drown out protest, yet a national uprising looms. The regime calls participants in its street spectacles – its “Islam Party” – fedayeen, echoing the political theater of Saddam Hussein and Muammar Gaddafi.
The Revolutionary Guards and security officials squander their days in endless meetings, terrified by the deepening crisis and sheltering behind a bankrupt, discredited government. Agriculture, industry, and production have ground to a halt. There is no coherent plan to regain control. The regime’s security calculations are unraveling.
Iranians await another war in the hope that the bloodthirsty wolf of the Islamic Republic will finally be brought down. They hope Trump will finish the job – or allow Israel to eliminate the regime’s thugs and criminals, layer by layer.
Meanwhile, the regime intensifies killings and executions, hoping to prevent economic misery, relentless inflation, soaring prices, and mounting social anguish from erupting into the “final battle.” Iran is passing through fateful days as urban repression intensifies. The regime’s ultimate nightmare is a popular uprising. A regime that kills its own people for daring to protest will stop at no crime to preserve its rule.
And yet, behind every headline about war, sanctions, missiles, and nuclear negotiations lies another Iran – the Iran of ordinary people who simply want to live. They want to raise their children without fear, put food on the table, walk their streets without repression, speak without looking over their shoulders, and grow old in the country they love.
For nearly half a century, generations of Iranians have watched their lives disappear into prisons, graves, exile, poverty, and shattered dreams. They are not asking the world to give them a country. They already have one – an ancient and beloved homeland called Iran.
They are asking for the chance to take it back. Ninety million people have waited long enough. In memory of the 50,000 slaughtered in Tehran’s streets by the Shi’ite mullahs and IRGC thugs, who cried out, “This is the final battle – Pahlavi will return!” Iran deserves to live again. “Make Iran Great Again!”
Let us hope Washington has the resolve and unwavering will to make it happen.
The writer is a Middle East political analyst. His latest book, Tehran’s Dictator, examines the theocratic era of Ali Khamenei (1989-2026). @EQFard

articles.title: Russia enlists criminal groups to carry out attacks on the heads of European defense companies – FT
articles.body:
Russia enlists criminal groups to carry out attacks on the heads of European defense companies – FT
Kyiv • UNN
Russian special services are preparing attacks on the heads of European defense companies, enlisting organized criminal groups. The goal is to intimidate businesses and weaken support for Ukraine.
Russian intelligence services have intensified preparations for assassination attempts targeting executives of European defense companies involved in the production of weapons and military equipment, including for Ukraine. UNN reports this, citing the Financial Times.
Details
According to the publication, which spoke with representatives of five European intelligence services, the Kremlin is stepping up sabotage activities in Europe in an attempt to weaken military support for Ukraine. Potential targets of Russian intelligence services may include executives of major defense corporations, as well as smaller companies producing drones, components, and other military equipment for the Ukrainian army.
European intelligence services are particularly concerned about the change in methods used to conduct Russian operations. According to FT's sources, Russian military intelligence is increasingly involving members of organized criminal groups in preparing acts of sabotage and possible assassinations.
Previously, recruits approached via the internet and offered financial rewards were actively used to carry out such tasks. Now, according to intelligence assessments, the organization of operations is becoming more complex, with individual stages of preparation potentially being carried out by different groups in several countries.
The publication's sources claim that European law enforcement and intelligence agencies have already detected and thwarted individual plots. There have also been cases of suspicious surveillance of potential victims near their homes and workplaces. Amid the rising threats, a number of European defense companies have introduced additional security measures. Some executives are under round-the-clock protection, while during trips abroad they use the services of specialized security teams.
According to FT's sources, the aim of such actions is to intimidate Europe's defense industry. The constant threat of attacks could increase companies' security costs and complicate their cooperation with Ukraine.
Context
One of the best-known cases was the reported preparation of an assassination attempt against Armin Papperger, CEO of the German defense contractor Rheinmetall. In July 2024, Western media reported on a Russian plan to kill him. In January 2025, NATO official James Appathurai confirmed that there had been a threat to the life of the company's head and also reported other similar plots against representatives of the defense industry.
In addition, on October 5, 2026, the heads of Germany's intelligence agencies warned during hearings in the Bundestag about an intensification of Russia's hybrid operations. In particular, they referred to threats of sabotage, acts of violence, and attacks on the defense industry and critical infrastructure.
On October 7, Denmark's Security and Intelligence Service also reported attempts to carry out sabotage against Danish companies supplying weapons to Ukraine. According to the agency's assessment, Russian entities are increasingly directing their operations against production facilities whose activities directly affect the Ukrainian army's military capabilities.
Reminder
U.S. prosecutors exposed an alleged global network of Russian intelligence services, whose members are accused of preparing assassinations and acts of sabotage in the United States and Europe. The U.S. Department of Justice charged five individuals, who remain at large.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition says 'unidentified projectile' targeted Terminal 4 at Riyadh airport
articles.body:
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said an "unidentified projectile" had targeted Riyadh's international airport on Sunday, causing a fire, hours after the Iran-backed Houthis warned airlines and travelers to stay away from Saudi airports.
The coalition also said Saudi air defenses had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport. No further details were immediately available.
The airport remains closed after an attack there on Saturday killed 12 people and wounded more than 300 others, the deadliest such strike on the kingdom in over a decade, amid an escalation of fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces.
The Indian Embassy in Riyadh confirmed on Sunday that one of the 12 killed in Saturday's strike was an Indian national.
Despite the airport's temporary closure, the Saudi Energy Ministry said a long-planned international energy conference was still going ahead in Riyadh on Sunday.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said Sunday's projectile had targeted Terminal 4 of the airport, without elaborating.
Earlier, the Houthis had said in a statement on X:
"We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our forces, with the exception of the airports in (the holy cities of) Mecca and Medina."
"We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions."
Houthis warn, 'Worse is yet to come,'
Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
Yemen's Houthi-run foreign ministry said later on Sunday that further Saudi military action in Yemen would trigger a stronger response, adding that its actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity.
"Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the ministry said in statements carried by Houthi-run Al Masirah television.
President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war on Iran that the US and Israel launched in February.
International energy conference still going ahead
A five-day WPC Energy Congress is taking place this week at a convention center some 10 km (6 miles) from the airport. State TV said more than 70 ministers, 300 company executives and representatives of over 25 international energy organizations had confirmed their attendance.
It was not immediately clear whether the participants would attend in person or virtually.
A ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum is also set to go ahead on Sunday, with its plenary session to be held behind closed doors, according to a media advisory. No further details were immediately available.
Separately, Saudi authorities notified parents that in-person classes would be suspended and shifted to remote learning from Sunday until Thursday for all students, teachers and administrative staff.
In Saturday's attack, the third on Riyadh's airport in a week, the 12 dead included 4 Saudis, 2 Bangladeshis and nationals of the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, Saudi authorities said.
Four people were killed in the two previous attacks on the airport earlier in the week. One of the attacks also caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.

articles.title: British startup develops 100-mile strike missile
articles.body:
- British startup Cody Aerospace & Defence unveiled the Badger Mk1 strike missile, with a 70- to 100-mile range and up to 100 kg warhead.
- The missile is in design, the company is raising pre-seed funding, and it targets development maturity within 18 months to two years.
Cody Aerospace & Defence, a British company founded in February, has unveiled its first product, the Badger Mk1 ground-launched strike missile, along with plans for a factory to build it and a goal of replenishing stockpiles in under a year.
The company announced the missile at the Apex Europe defense show in London this week. It says Badger Mk1 will fly 70 to 100 miles (about 110 to 160 km) and carry a warhead of up to 100 kg (220 pounds), and that it is aimed at NATO members and allied armies as a ground-to-ground indirect fire weapon. The missile would launch from a converted ISO shipping container, sold together with radar and fire control so a customer buys a complete system.
Badger is still in the design phase, and Cody is raising pre-seed capital. Founder Henry Price told the UK Defence Journal the company wants to bring the missile to development maturity, including testing, within 18 months to two years, using seekers, rocket motors and guidance systems bought off the shelf from existing suppliers. Cody has not announced any customers, a unit price or test dates.
Cody also announced Ordnance One, the factory where it plans to build Badger. The company says the plant would also produce other companies’ and countries’ weapons under license. It has not said where the factory will be built or how much it will cost.
Price, who spent 15 years at large defense contractors and their main suppliers before founding Cody, said the company’s pitch rests on stockpile numbers.
“If you look at the problem statement of seven to ten days of stockpiles on the shelf for the UK in intensive warfare, and three years to replace it, that’s all we need to solve,” said Price.
He said Cody is aiming for a replenishment cycle of under a year once the missile is in production, compared with the roughly three years he says it takes to replace stocks bought off the shelf from the United States. He added that U.S. defense orders carry priority ratings that generally put American customers first, which he said can stretch delivery to four or five years. Cody also plans to add an interceptor missile to the same container launcher “a couple of years” after Badger, giving one vehicle both strike and air defense roles.
Price said Cody is lining up British suppliers for explosives and rocket motors, but acknowledged that rare earths and composites depend on supply chains Europe does not fully control. He said a fully British supply chain would cost three to four times as much, according to suppliers.
“I want engineers to be delivering capability, not managing obsolescence,” said Price.
He also argued that NATO should standardize rocket munitions so any similar-sized round can be fired from different allied launchers, and said Cody’s software and fire control will be open source.
The UK government has been trying to rebuild weapons stocks since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Price said the Defence Investment Plan set aside £11.1 billion (about $14.8 billion) for stockpiles and that Cody wants to help the Ministry of Defence spend it more efficiently. Another British startup, Cambridge Aerospace, has already moved from founding to a Ministry of Defence order for its Skyhammer interceptor in less than two years.

articles.title: Russia equips Geran attack drones with image-based navigation using Google map imagery, reducing reliance on satellite navigation that Ukraine can jam, defense adviser warns
articles.body:
Russia is developing new navigation systems for attack drones and missiles that could make its strikes against Ukrainian cities harder to stop, as Moscow adapts its weapons to counter Ukrainian electronic warfare defenses, Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said.
The shift poses an additional challenge for Ukraine as Russia continues to attack cities and critical infrastructure with drones and missiles. Systems that can navigate without relying on satellite signals may be harder to disrupt electronically, increasing the importance of other defenses, including interception and physical destruction of incoming weapons.
Image-based navigation could make Russian strike drones harder to jam
Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president on defense technology development, said image-based navigation systems would see wider use in 2027, including in medium- and long-range strike drones and inexpensive cruise missiles.
The technology allows drones to navigate by comparing images captured by an onboard camera with stored photographs of the terrain. Even basic navigation can use publicly available satellite or ground imagery from services such as Google, Beskrestnov said.
Unlike satellite navigation, which can be disrupted by electronic warfare, image-based navigation relies on visual recognition of the terrain. This makes drones using the technology more resistant to jamming and could allow them to continue toward their targets even when satellite navigation signals are unavailable.
Russia already uses image-based navigation on attack drones
Beskrestnov said Russian forces were already using the technology on several types of unmanned aircraft, including Molniya, V2U, and Lancet drones.
He also reported that similar systems had recently been identified on the Russian Geran-4 and Geran-5 attack drones, using a flight controller called Susanin.
The Geran series includes Russian attack drones used in strikes against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. The introduction of image-based navigation could make some variants more difficult for Ukrainian forces to counter using electronic warfare.
Russia adapts its weapons to Ukrainian defenses
The development reflects Russia’s broader effort to adapt its weapons as Ukraine improves its air defenses and electronic warfare capabilities. By reducing reliance on satellite navigation signals, Russian drones can become less vulnerable to one of Ukraine’s key methods of disrupting incoming attacks.
Beskrestnov warned that image-based navigation would expand beyond individual drone models, with broader adoption expected next year across different categories of strike weapons.

articles.title: Russia and Ukraine agree to energy ceasefire – Trump
articles.body:
Russia and Ukraine agree to energy ceasefire – Trump
US President Donald Trump has said Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire. The announcement comes just days after Trump’s phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, during which the two leaders agreed on a deal aimed at easing the global fuel crisis through Russian diesel exports.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday, adding that “both parties have agreed” and urging Moscow and Kiev not to “break it.”
Ukraine's Vladimir Zelensky later confirmed on X that he discussed Trump’s announcement with NATO chief Mark Rutte, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, adding that Kiev supports the initiative.
Moscow has not commented on Trump’s announcement so far.
On Friday, Trump and Putin held a phone call, shortly after which the US Treasury Department announced a temporary waiver of sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing the fuel to be sold, delivered, and imported into the US until April 7, 2027.
According to Trump, Moscow agreed to immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 metric tons in November and one million more shortly thereafter. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak also confirmed the figures and said Moscow would begin lifting diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule “immediately.”
The US president allegedly struck a deal with Moscow after Zelensky ignored Washington’s requests to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, Axios reported on Saturday. Trump has blamed Ukraine, and Zelensky personally, for exacerbating the global fuel crisis, saying that Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have driven up fuel prices, including for American consumers.
On Saturday, Trump once again accused Zelensky of seeking to “make problems for the world” and ignoring US requests, suggesting that it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.” The Ukrainian leader hit back by demanding a two-month-long total ceasefire to hold the vote.
“If President Trump really wants to have some changes during elections… please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections,” he told ABC on Sunday.
Russia considers Zelensky illegitimate, as his presidential term expired more than two years ago and he has not called a new election, citing martial law.
Ukraine has ramped up long-range strikes on targets inside Russia, including civilian and energy infrastructure such as oil refineries, amid continued setbacks at the front. Zelensky has recently threatened to intensify attacks on Russian refineries in particular. Moscow has denounced the attacks as acts of terrorism and vowed to intensify strikes on Ukrainian military-related facilities, including drone and missile warehouses, while maintaining that it never targets civilians.

articles.title: Ukraine has imposed new sanctions against the manufacturers of "Iskander" and "Zircon" missiles and financial intermediaries of the Russian Federation

Ukraine has imposed new sanctions against the manufacturers of "Iskander" and "Zircon" missiles and financial intermediaries of the Russian Federation
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy signed three decrees imposing sanctions against missile manufacturers, financial intermediaries of the Russian Federation, and figures in the occupied territories. The restrictions apply to 107 individuals, 48 companies, and two vessels.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed three decrees imposing sanctions against individuals and companies that ensure the production of Russian missiles, help Moscow circumvent international restrictions, and operate in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. This was reported by the Office of the President, writes UNN.
Details
The first sanctions package covers 70 Russian citizens, including engineers, technologists, and executives of enterprises involved in the production of Iskander-M ballistic missiles and Zircon hypersonic missiles.
The second package targets 28 individuals and 27 legal entities that, according to the Ukrainian side, help Russia circumvent financial sanctions. The list includes, in particular, cryptocurrency exchange operators and participants in the shadow banking network A7.
Companies and maritime vessels were also subjected to restrictions
The third sanctions package concerns activities in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. It includes 10 individuals and 21 legal entities, as well as two maritime vessels that, according to the Office of the President, operate in Russia's interests.
Thus, the new restrictions cover several areas at once — from Russia's military-industrial complex to financial schemes for circumventing sanctions and economic activity in the occupied territories.

articles.title: Russia is building jet drones that fly 800 kilometers per hour, and Ukraine says it is already working on how to stop next generation
articles.body:
Aviation is one of the most effective ways to counter Russia’s jet-powered drones. Its effectiveness continues to grow due to pilots’ skill and better coordination, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara says, Glavcom reports.
Russia’s jet-powered Gerans fly several times faster than the propeller Shaheds Ukraine learned to shoot down, and they remain the main challenge for its air defense. Ukraine downs more than 90% of the slow drones but only about 55% of the jet ones.
“Due to them, our aviation now uses fewer munitions per aerial target. We plan to improve this further,” Khmara states.
Air defense works as a layered system because no single type of weapon is enough, he explains. The layers run from surface-to-air and shoulder-fired missiles to turrets, electronic warfare, interceptor-drone crews, and small-scale air defense, topped by aircraft including Mirage and F-16 jets.
Scaling what works against jet drones
Ukraine already has combat results against the jet drones, Khmara notes. In one engagement, five Bars interceptors destroyed five aerial targets, a 100% hit rate in that case, and the task now is to raise the overall destruction rate and quickly scale the solutions that prove themselves.
Heavy-caliber turrets are adding to that. Their number in service already runs into the hundreds, he adds.
“This direction is being scaled, and systems with greater range are being worked on. In parallel, surface-to-air and shoulder-fired missile systems are also proving effective,” he says.
Preparing for the next generation
Ukraine is also looking past today’s threats, the minister stresses. The ministry is working to supply interceptor drones, aviation and its munitions, missile and artillery systems, turrets and electronic warfare gear, and to plan several steps ahead with enough stock in reserve.
“We also know what solutions Russia is developing, which concern jet drones with a speed of 800 kilometers per hour. We are working on finding countermeasures to the next generation of threats,” Khmara says.
Producers have been tasked with offering proposals and prototypes, he concludes.

articles.title: Pentagon raises US-Iran war toll to 21 killed, over 800 wounded
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Pentagon raises US-Iran war toll to 21 killed, over 800 wounded
The US Department of War has raised the death toll of US personnel in its war on Iran to 21 killed and 865 wounded in an acknowledgement that losses faced during the conflict were greater than previously admitted.
The Pentagon added two non-combatant deaths, including one Major who died in Kuwait on 6 March and a Navy suicide from September, according to The Washington Post.
The publication previously reported in September that the department's internal figures counted 23 service members as having died since the start of the war on 28 February.
The admission is a firm rebuttal of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, who previously labelled the reporting of a higher death toll as “a complete lie", as well as a correction of previous reporting by the Pentagon, which has underreported the toll since the start of the war due to Trump's own claims that the war has ended.
In a bid to mark deaths in the region tied to continued war with Iran, the department created a new category for those killed after Trump’s declaration.
The Pentagon told The Post in a statement that, rather than correcting its own figures, it is making revisions to how it reports casualties.
The number of US casualties in its war on Iran have been contentious, with US media outlets revealing larger casualty figures than admitted to by the Pentagon throughout the war.
Despite US and Israeli airpower decapitating Iran's leadership and destroying vast swathes of Iranian military assets, Iran's quick response saw ballistic missiles and drones targeting US bases, alongside Iran's Gulf neighbours and Israel.
Iranian attacks on US bases have left the 5th Fleet headquarters in Bahrain and Al Udeid Air Base, the largest US airbase in the region, severely damaged.
Iranian attacks also damaged or destroyed US radar used to track ballistic missiles and aircraft on the ground.
The extent of the damage has led the Department of War to mull pulling troops and withdrawing from bases in the Gulf.
However, in recent weeks, Trump ordered new plans to be drawn up for renewed strikes against Iran, as negotiatons between the two reach an impasse.

articles.title: A ‘Cold Fish’ Who ‘Never Made Eye Contact’ – Former UK PM on Putin
articles.body:
Former UK Prime Minister Theresa May reflected this week on her encounters with Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump, changes in the White House media environment, and what she believes those changes meant for President Volodymyr Zelensky’s explosive exchange with Trump in the Oval Office in February 2024.
May was interviewed at the Henley Literature Festival in the UK on Oct. 8, as part of a special recording of The Independent’s political podcast “In the Room,” which examines what really goes on inside the rooms where decisions are made.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Reflecting on her time in Downing Street, May said of Putin, “Once a KGB man, always a KGB man,” reiterating the words she used in a Sky News interview on July 30, 2026, in which she also said “it cannot be business as usual with Russia.”
Recalling in the Henley podcast what it was like to come face-to-face with global leaders and sit across the table from Putin at Group of 20 (G20) meetings, she said Putin “wouldn’t make eye contact with anybody” and was a “completely cold fish.”
“As prime minister, you meet other world leaders and you have to take them as you find them,” May said.
“In Putin, I will say, once a KGB man, always a KGB man. He was a completely cold fish and one of the things I noticed particularly at G20 meetings when we were all sitting around the table was, he just wouldn’t make eye contact with anybody. He was sort of like this the whole time, but obviously we had very limited relations with Russia post Salisbury, and we’d had fairly limited relations before.”
Trump: Putin Wants Ukraine Deal, Praises Russian Oil Supplies
May’s remarks referred to Russian military intelligence officer Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia, who were found slumped on a park bench in Salisbury, England, after being exposed to the Novichok nerve agent. The UK government concluded in September 2018 that the poisoning – which the Skripals survived but which led to the death of Salisbury resident Dawn Sturgess – was “almost certainly” approved by the Russian state.
May added that she had always been “a bit of a Russia hawk” during her tenure as Home Secretary and said that the UK “hadn’t properly” responded to the killing of Alexander Litvinenko, which was always “hanging over” relations.
Litvinenko was a British-naturalised Russian defector and former officer of the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) who was poisoned with polonium-210 in late 2006 and died as a result in a London hospital on Nov. 23 that year.
On Trump and the White House media machine
Turning to Trump, May remarked jovially, “I think I’m probably the only world leader whose hand he’s held,” referring to her official visit to the White House on Jan. 27, 2017, when the two leaders walked along the White House Colonnade. As reported at the time by UK newspaper The Guardian, the gesture “surprised” British officials and prompted a flurry of international media coverage.
May went on to say that – in her view – Trump is “different” in his second term from his first, appearing to link this to changes in both the conduct of traditional set-piece meetings and the people surrounding the US president.
“I think he was able to have four years when he was out of office, thinking about what he really wanted to do and about who he wanted to have around him,” May said.
“There were some very key people around him in the first administration who were old hands if you like – some would say the establishment – who sort of knew about the way that most of these relations were conducted.”
May described Oval Office meetings for which leaders would traditionally be briefed to “say warm words,” for example about “strengthening the relationship,” after which cameras would be ushered out of the room and a private meeting would begin.
May then likened more recent meetings during Trump’s second term to “a TV show” and expressed disappointment with the way Zelensky was treated during his fiery Oval Office encounter with Trump on Feb. 28, 2024.
“It’s a TV show now as we saw sadly with the way President Zelensky was treated on the first visit… the cameras are in there during this… they’re able to ask questions so it’s an entirely different environment.”
The February 2024 verbal clash between Trump and Zelensky erupted over ceasefire terms, the management of the war, a paused rare-earth minerals deal, and demands from the US administration for more “gratitude” from Ukraine for US military aid.

articles.title: Elon Musk Echoes Trump in Calling for New Ukrainian Leadership
articles.body:
American billionaire Elon Musk endorsed US President Donald Trump’s statements calling for a change in Ukraine’s leadership, writing on X that President Volodymyr Zelensky had “gone too far.”
Musk made the remarks while commenting on video footage of Trump criticizing Zelensky for failing to finalize a negotiated settlement with Russia despite having multiple opportunities to do so.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In the video, Trump asserted that the Ukrainian electorate should select a new president capable of reaching an agreement with Moscow.
Musk’s post marks the latest in a series of public criticisms directed at the Ukrainian head of state.
In February 2025, the tech entrepreneur claimed that Ukrainians held unfavorable views of Zelensky, and in March 2025, he called for national elections in Ukraine, asserting that the incumbent president would lose.
Zelensky has gone too far
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 10, 2026
Trump’s remarks and criticism of refinery strikes
Musk’s comments align with a public defense mounted by Trump on Saturday regarding a bilateral commercial diesel agreement reached with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Speaking to reporters roughly a month before the US midterm elections as retail diesel prices approached $6 per gallon, Trump blamed Ukraine’s long-range strikes against Russian oil refineries for causing disruptions across international energy and agricultural markets.
“He wants to make problems for the world, for our farmers with diesel,” Trump told reporters, arguing that Zelensky had prolonged the war unnecessarily.
US Envoys Witkoff, Kushner May Visit Russia Soon
“Zelensky could have settled this war many, many times, but he chooses not to,” Trump said, renewing his calls for political change in Kyiv. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
The US president’s calls for a leadership transition in Kyiv drew a rebuttal from Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, who affirmed on Sunday that only the Ukrainian electorate holds the legal and sovereign authority to determine national governance during wartime. Sybiha stated that external criticism only demonstrates that Zelensky is performing his duties effectively, emphasizing that the Ukrainian head of state retains broad public support.
Trump’s comments followed his announcement on Friday, Oct. 9, of a commercial arrangement with Putin under which Moscow agreed to deliver over 300,000 metric tons of diesel immediately, scaling up to 1 million tons in subsequent phases through 2027.
To facilitate the shipments, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary sanctions waiver running through April 2027.
The diesel deal was announced while a Ukrainian delegation was engaged in multilateral security consultations with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami. Zelensky described the Miami talks as a “smokescreen” for bilateral economic concessions to the Kremlin.
Under the framework promoted by the administration, Kyiv has been urged to unilaterally halt drone interdiction operations against Russian oil refineries to stabilize fuel benchmarks.
However, the proposal contained no reciprocal condition requiring the Russian military to halt missile and drone strikes against Ukraine’s power and heating infrastructure.
Officials in Kyiv have reiterated that Ukraine will not suspend its asymmetric campaign against Russian refining installations without an enforceable, mutual energy ceasefire.
Ukrainian lawmakers and foreign policy officials have emphasized that degrading Russian downstream energy hubs remains necessary to constrain fuel supplies for Russian military operations and diminish state revenues funding the Kremlin’s wartime budget.

articles.title: How Israel's pager operation shattered Nasrallah’s aura of invincibility - opinion
articles.body:
The second anniversary of the pager operation is a reminder that the first thing to explode on September 17, 2024, was not thousands of small devices. It was the carefully cultivated aura of invulnerability that Hassan Nasrallah had built around himself.
For years, the Hezbollah leader had appeared from his hideout, boasting about missiles, tunnels, and “surprises,” asking the Lebanese to believe that his disappearance was strategic brilliance. The terrorist group could see without being seen, strike without being touched.
Then an old-fashioned device exposed the reality. The organization that had cowed Lebanon through fear had been compromised through its own supply chain. Its leader, who threatened to bury his enemies, did not know his men were carrying booby-trapped devices.
This was not simply an intelligence coup worthy of a spy thriller. Israeli intelligence had constructed a false reality in which Hezbollah operated with complete confidence. Public investigations and the book In the War Room trace the idea’s origins to 2002-2006, during Meir Dagan’s tenure.
Around 2014, Mossad and Israeli military intelligence began introducing wireless devices into Hezbollah’s network, monitoring them while retaining the option of detonation. In 2022, they turned to pagers: devices operatives would carry rather than leave in an office or warehouse.
Front companies, licensing arrangements, dummy websites, and stores gave a battery unavailable on the open market a convincing commercial identity. A Taiwanese brand and a supply chain stretching from Hungary to Hong Kong supplied the cover. The Mossad did not simply intercept a shipment. It created the product, marketed it, built its reputation, and cut the price until Hezbollah’s procurement officials chose the trap themselves.
This was the difference between penetrating an organization and shaping the choices it believed were its own. The procurement process offered the appearance of control while delivering precisely what the adversary wanted.
They thought they were vetting a product. In reality, the product was exposing the organization.
Explosives were built into the batteries
A Reuters investigation found that explosives and a concealed detonator were built into the battery, allowing the devices to pass Hezbollah’s security checks. Even when officials noticed that batteries drained faster than advertised, distribution continued.
The message and alert were designed to make recipients bring the device toward their faces and use both hands. The alert tone and explosive charge had been tested to produce the intended response. The Mossad had choreographed the movements of those carrying its bombs.
The bitterest irony was that Nasrallah himself helped the operation. In February 2024, he called mobile phones more dangerous than spies and urged his men to smash them, bury them, or lock them in metal boxes. Hezbollah accelerated its adoption of pagers. His warning did not create the operation, but it drove more men toward the prepared device. The leadership’s fear had become a predictable procurement decision. Hezbollah had chosen its own poisoned remedy.
I see something deeper here than a procurement mistake. An entire security doctrine collapsed: secrecy supposedly meant switching off a phone, while the enemy was manufacturing the alternative.
At 3:30 p.m. on September 17, the devices began to ring. Roughly 3,000 exploded. The next day came the wireless devices, some held by Hezbollah for nearly a decade. Dozens were killed and more than 3,400 wounded. Devices had been distributed among fighters, commanders, support personnel, and affiliated medics. The penetration even reached Iran’s ambassador. The target was the infrastructure that enabled an Iranian-backed militia to operate as a state within Lebanon.
More important, in my view, was the assault on trust. Anyone still carrying a device had reason to fear its battery. Those who watched colleagues fall simultaneously understood that the enemy had helped build the walls behind which they sheltered. The equipment meant to connect the organization had become a source of fear. Replacing it could restore communication, but could not erase the discovery that trusted channels had carried the enemy inside.
Two former Mossad officers described the intended psychological impact. Wafiq Safa, a close Nasrallah associate, later recounted that the attacks left him deeply shaken and barely eating for almost a day. The man who had spent his life instilling fear in the Lebanese discovered, days before his death, that fear had reached his own hideout.
The operation also opened a military campaign. On September 20, Ibrahim Aqil and Radwan Force commanders were killed. Strikes expanded to weapons depots, facilities, and positions. On September 27, Nasrallah was killed beneath the headquarters he had regarded as an impregnable fortress.
Intelligence derives its real power from turning secrets into paralysis and confusion at the moment military force can exploit them. Without the subsequent strikes, the explosions would have remained an extraordinary intelligence feat. Their succession made the operation the opening phase of a broader dismantling.
Nasrallah had built his authority on the belief that obscurity proved knowledge, disappearance meant immunity, and questioning the leadership betrayed resistance. The farther he withdrew, the more formidable he appeared. Secrecy became wisdom beyond scrutiny.
The pagers exposed what that mythology concealed. His disappearance was isolation. His secrecy hid ignorance of what entered his warehouses. His speeches promised deterrence while his security apparatus was already penetrated.
That is the weakness of closed ideological organizations. They confuse loyalty with competence and treat questions as betrayal. Eventually, the leader’s word becomes a vulnerability no one dares challenge. A professional intelligence service could engineer the environment around its target; a terrorist militia had mistaken suspicion and obedience for security.
Two years later, Hezbollah can buy devices, change intermediaries, and rebuild parts of its network. It cannot turn the clock back to before the first ring.
The militia that claimed to protect Lebanon could not even protect its own supply chain. The leader who threatened to bury his enemies was himself buried beneath the concrete, along with the project he had built. And the Shi’ite community asked to believe in divine protection saw that an aura of sanctity could neither stop a signal nor reveal a compromised battery.
The most devastating part was that Hezbollah’s own leadership had led its men, step by step, to the very tool Israel designed to reach them. In doing so, it shattered the image of Nasrallah as an infallible leader.
The writer is a UAE political analyst and former Federal National Council candidate.

articles.title: Ukraine ready to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries if Russia stops attacking energy infrastructure — Zelensky
articles.body:
Ukraine ready to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries if Russia stops attacking energy infrastructure — Zelensky
According to Ukrinform, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said this in a Facebook post, commenting on Russian attacks against Ukraine over the past week.
"I am grateful to all our emergency services, who are always there for our people and work to address the aftermath of brutal Russian strikes. Only this morning, search and rescue operations were completed in Zaporizhzhia, where Russia killed 23 people, including four children. Yesterday, the Russians struck a medical facility in Kharkiv, and overnight there were Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure, residential buildings, and energy infrastructure. This morning, the Russians struck a five-story apartment building in Slovyansk – an entire section of the building was destroyed, and people may still be under the rubble," Zelensky said.
According to the president, Russia launched approximately 1,450 guided aerial bombs, 75 missiles of various types, and more than 1,640 attack drones over the past week alone. About 60% of the drones were jet-powered.
"Today, we will continue coordinating with partners – there will be talks with European leaders. Virtually every day, we coordinate at different levels and work on additional defense packages, first and foremost air defense and munitions for combat aircraft. All of this is to protect the lives of our people and Ukraine's interests," Zelensky emphasized.
He added that Russia—and Russia alone—is the real cause of the war in Europe.
"It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so. Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure. Any de-escalation steps must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees," Zelensky stressed.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Axios, citing a U.S. official, wrote that U.S. President Donald Trump had decided to strike a deal with Russia on diesel fuel after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky refused to unilaterally halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.

articles.title: Zelenskyy claps back after Trump calls for new Ukrainian president
articles.body:
Trump announces Russia-Ukraine "energy ceasefire" after calling for Zelenskyy's replacement
President Trump said Sunday that Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an "energy ceasefire," shortly after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy vowed to continue striking Russian oil refineries in response to criticism from Mr. Trump.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Mr. Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
It's unclear exactly what the ceasefire entails, and Zelenskyy told Axios after Mr. Trump's announcement that the ceasefire "was news for me." But the Ukrainian president said Ukraine would agree to a ceasefire if Russia were to also agree.
CBS News has reached out to the White House for clarity on the agreement.
Mr. Trump previously took aim at the Ukrainian president's leadership, suggesting Zelenskyy should be replaced and blaming him for high diesel prices. The Ukrainian president clapped back, saying Russia alone was responsible for the war in Ukraine.
"Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure," Zelenskyy wrote on X.
"It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but (Russian President Vladimir) Putin does not want to do so," he said, adding that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees.
The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center run by Russian technology giant Yandex, the third strike on the company's facilities in four days. Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow's full-scale invasion.
Speaking to ABC News' "This Week" on Sunday morning, Zelenskyy said Ukrainians "want peace."
"About energy, I said it to President Trump ... to his team and to his people several times. We want peace," Zelenskyy said. "We are ready for ceasefire. We are ready to begin from any kind of steps of de-escalation."
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has also pushed back on Mr. Trump's comments, writing on X late Saturday that Zelenskyy was leading the country through a war for its independence.
"He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well," Sybiha wrote.
Mr. Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does," Mr. Trump said.
According to an announcement from Mr. Trump on Friday, the U.S. has made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy more than 300,000 tons of diesel from Russia right away, followed by 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons after that. Amid the deal, which attempts to address high fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, Mr. Trump has also urged Zelenskyy for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. Zelenskyy criticized the deal and said it would help fund Russia's war in Ukraine. 
Mr. Trump has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia's war effort.
The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, caused outages across the company's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.
"As a result of the drone attack, the infrastructure of Yandex's data center in Vladimir was damaged. Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries," said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which provides operational updates on service availability.
In Moscow, residents described disruption to everyday tasks. Pavel Belyavskiy, a driver for Yandex Taxi, said it was unclear whether orders were coming through at all, and that on several rides he had to cancel after waiting a long time because he could not reach the passenger.
"I'd press the 'call' button to contact them, but nothing happens," he said. "There's nothing I can do, so I'm just forced to cancel."
Igor Mann said he went to check the status of an order on the Yandex Market shopping platform but the page was unavailable, and connecting through a VPN did not help. "Nothing worked," he said.
Another Moscow resident, Eduard Malyavko, said the outages had "direct impact" and weren't just about "convenience."
"It's also about work," he said, adding that they also affected "healthcare, and everything else."
On Thursday, a drone attack took a Yandex data center offline in the Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow. A day later, Ukrainian drones hit the company's major data center in the Kaluga region, southwest of Moscow, partly putting it out of action, Yandex said.
Yandex, often described as Russia's Google, runs the country's most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia's artificial intelligence development.
Elsewhere, Zelenskyy said search and rescue operations ended in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia after a Russian bombing on Saturday.
Zelenskyy said 23 people were killed in the attack, including four children. More than 30 people were wounded, Fedorov said, eight of whom remain hospitalized.
A man was killed and two women wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike on Russia's Bryansk border region, local officials said Sunday.

articles.title: Riyadh vows response to airport attack, Yemen strike reported
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia on Sunday extended the closure of the country’s main international airport, according to an online flight tracker, a day after a missile attack on the facility killed 12 people from several countries and left more than 300 injured in a major escalation of the war between Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom.
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility in a televised speech for Saturday’s attack on Riyadh's international airport that killed 12 people and wounded more than 300 others.
Yemen's Houthis on Sunday renewed their warning to airlines, airport workers, and travellers against using Saudi airports, saying the warning should be taken seriously and that the kingdom "bore responsibility for failed interceptions".
Two Indian sailors missing after vessel attacked off Oman
Two Indian sailors were missing after a commercial vessel was hit by a "drone attack" Sunday off the coast of Oman, New Delhi's shipping minister said.
Shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal said the tanker MT Petro Dolphin, with 11 Indian seafarers on board, was attacked at the anchorage area for the port of Sohar in northern Oman.
"While nine of our Indian crew members have been successfully rescued and are safe, two Indian nationals currently remain missing," he said on X.
Sonowal said search and rescue operations by local authorities was underway.
"We are continuously coordinating with all relevant authorities to fully support the ongoing rescue efforts and ensure every possible action is taken to safely locate our missing personnel," he said.
Sonowal also said the Marshall Islands-flagged tanker M/T Valthera, carrying 11 Indian crew, was struck Sunday by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz. A fire was sparked, but all Indian crew were reported to be safe.
India is one of the largest contributors of sailors to merchant shipping worldwide, with more than 320,000 active seafarers in 2025, according to the shipping ministry.
Indian national injured in Riyadh airport attack dies
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said on Sunday that an Indian national injured in the attack at Riyadh's international airport had died.
"We are in touch with the family and will provide all support for ensuring the early repatriation of mortal remains," the embassy said in a post on X.
The Indian national's death adds to the death toll from the attack at Riyadh's international airport on Saturday, which killed 12 people according to initial reports and wounded more than 300 others, the deadliest such strike on Saudi Arabia in over a decade.
Netanyahu condemns 'horrific' attack on Riyadh airport
ICC fugitive Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday condemned the "horrific terrorist attack" on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia a day earlier.

AFP journalists heard a powerful blast in central Riyadh but the cause was not immediately clear.
France on Sunday called on Palestinian leaders to go back on their decision postponing legislative elections to next year.
The delay "deprives the Palestinian people of their right to democratically express themselves at the ballot box" for the first national elections in two decades, the French foreign ministry said in a statement.
Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas on Saturday pushed back the legislative vote, which had been scheduled for November 28, to September next year, alongside a presidential poll.
Russia condemns Riyadh airport attack, calls for diplomacy
The Russian Foreign Ministry said on Sunday that it condemned the attack on Riyadh airport, Russian news agency Interfax reported.
The situation in the Middle East can only be resolved through diplomatic means, while taking into account the interests of all countries in the region, the ministry said.
France condemns 'heinous attack' by Houthis on airport
